"This game is amazing! Building your own robots and fighting others to win. I hope I have enough levels to get the wings!" That is what I said about a year ago. That was when Robocraft was amazing. It was a balanced system that allowed you to buy the parts you need to build a robot. Once you gain enough experience, you could make your robot bigger and with better components. You would get money and experience based on how well you played, and you would be in matchmaking with robots around the same level as you.
THIS WAS A YEAR AGO.
After the so called "Big Expansion," the rewards AND matchmaking sytems completely changed. Getting a good robot is hardly based on skill, but rather on luck. You don't need to be a certain level to get hi-tier parts, but can buy them from the shop immedeately or getting lucky from a rewards crate. The system has changed so that you can only get new parts by selling the old parts and buying new ones, or getting lucky with a rewards crate. No longer does the game reward skill, but rewards luck. You can no longer recieve money from matches, but different rewards crates that give you different chances on getting good items. Now you can gamble your REAL MONEY on rewards crates instead of getting what you need.
The matchmaking also changed. There used to be a ranking on each part of the robot as to how good it is. This accumulated for all parts of your robot and matched you with similarly outfitted robots. Instead, robots are measured by how much is put onto them. In doing so, matches have become very unbalanced because of the differences in weaponry. The devs of this game faded away from the idea of making Robocraft "The Awesome Robot Brawling Game," and instead pursued, "How can we make more money?" and, "How can we get the best stats on Steam?" Because of their greed, this may be the last year that Robocraft is running. Many people (including myself) will probably stop playing this until it is restored to its former glory.
I certainly hope they revert to the previous version.

This is the Age of Empires you remember, completely unsullied, but now with the added benefit of the Steam Workshop, which allows not only the custom games of old but whatever crazy stuff people want to build for it now.  Additionally, there's been an expansion to this already, which means this game is getting active developer attention, so many years after its original release!  I'm pretty impressed.

I hate to have to get on the bandwagon, but the new update is an abomination on one of the most unique and potentially briliant games I've ever played. Loot crates are a terrible system in any game, but putting them in one like this that's focused so strongly on creativity is a joke. They need to go back to a currency based system that rewards players properly instead of at random. If they really feel the need to have one of these asinine "blind bag" systems that focus more on exploiting gambling addiction than any sort of fun, it should be secondary to a more reliable system of currency.. like the one they threw out.
I'm not sure what goes through the minds of the Robocraft devs, but I've never seen a game flail around so much in terms of its core systems. It's like the whole thing is just an experiment and they have no actual vision for what the game should be. Many of the things they've changed over the years have been improvements, but this one... if anything, it seems like a misguided marketing idea. I deeply hope they come back to what made Robocraft great some day, and stick with it.

The thing that I love about Age II is the balance. It's advanced enough to be strategically challenging, and simple enough to understand fundamentally what needs to be done with only a playthrough or two.

All before the enemy beats you to it, racing against time.
Grab some buddies and crank up the difficulty. You will know stress. And you'll have fun doing it.

Like many others my biggest problem with the game is the recent "epic loot" update.  The combat system is enjoyable, and I like the robot creation tools.  The problem is how difficult it is to get everything now.  With the currency system battles were rewarding;  a long battle may be more of a grind, but it would be that much more worthwhile because the reward was higher.  With the epic loot system it doesn't matter if a game takes 5 minutes or an hour, you get the same stuff.
The epic loot system also just doesn't feel rewarding to me, and I get protonium crates more often than not from battles.  You can recycle items you get from loot crates that you don't want but they recycle for such low prices that the feature's nearly useless.  I understand that there is the potential for a loot crate to be more valuable than the galaxy cash, but it has yet to happen for me.  At this point the daunting aspect of grinding until I can get the parts I want has just about driven me away.  I can only imagine how disappointing it must be for people who get rusted and bronze crates more often.
I can understand the inention to appeal to new players by making it easier to start the game with higher level loot, but it shouldn't come at the expense of the players that are already invested in the game.
At his point I'm still hanging in there in the hopes that it'll turn around, and would be more than happy to recommend the game if a future update adresses the current problems.

Robocraft used to be an awesome game.  It was casual and fun, but at the same time you could be tactical and competitive.  The game was just brimming with potential!  I was eagerly looking forward to seeing how the game developed.
Sadly, the game didn't go in a good way...

Essentially every update to the game involved changing large amounts of core features of the game.  Adding and removing entire game modes, bot categories, gear types, playstyles, etc.  They constantly are making broad sweeping changes that drastically alter the game. It gives the impression that Freejam doesn't actually have any overall plan for the games direction.
They'll be all about something one moment, they'll hype it up, paint a clear picture of how they see it becoming a big thing in the game, and then by the next two updates its completely phased out or largely unrecognizable.
They haven't added new maps for ages despite that being one of the most requested things.  Worse, the maps that do exist largely cater to specific bot designs and playstyles which leads to balancing issues since people will naturally flock to those bot designs.  They need more variety of maps and especially need some more closed in and close quarters maps to contrast with their current maps which are largely open craters with extremely long distance sight lines. A cramped entirely underground cave map would have been a treat to see, but I doubt that will ever happen.
Balance is another key issue with the game.  Often some parts or weapons will drastically be outclassed by another or heavily limited to their usage together or some things will be easily exploitable.  Freejam lets these things go for long periods of time and then as the problem grows out of hand they tend to hamfist a solution by adding in overpowered new things you can buy to counter the problem bots instead of fixing the actual imbalance.
A good example would be plasma bombing planes.  Plasma was one of the only actual useful weapons for planes so naturally people gravitated to it and there ended up being swarms of them.  Instead of adding maps with more air cover or making other weapons that are viable for air instead of primarily just plasma... they solved it by having a whole series of updates aimed solely at adding in weapons that could completely annihilate fliers.
Worst of all is that winged flyers, which were already weak compared to drones and helicopters, are now left at an even more drastic disadvantage. Balancing a game by releasing new items just to crush an entire playstyle instead of fixing the core issues is just a horrible solution.... good money for Freejam though with all the people buying the new toys.
To further add to the balance issues Freejam added in a shop where players can put their bot designs up for sale.  In theory this sounds like a good idea, but in practice it just means that as soon as an exploitative or "current updates best" bot design is found the store is flooded with them.  The game then quickly gets filled up with players using copies of them and every match becomes the same boring slog with no signs of creativity.  Even when there isn't a current game ruining exploit build thats popular there are still several designs which people consider "the best" you'll still end up playing essentially nothing but matches filled with copies.  If you're lucky... the people will have at least painted their store bought clone differently so it will almost give you the illusion of seeing new and interesting designs.
Bugs are another big complaint.  Bugs don't really seem to get fixed.  They are just ignored until that entire portion of the game gets replaced with their next massive core feature altering update.  It doesn't matter if the bugs are small and simple ones, such as the "your platoon is waiting for you to join the queue" beeping sound going off constantly when you're in a platoon, or large and game wrecking ones, such as players being able to get underneath the map and kill everyone or place parts in ways that shouldn't be possible, they rarely ever get addressed.
The final straw though... the "Epic Loot" update.  In the past you could make what you wanted because you earned points to buy things with every round.  Now its almost entirely gambling.  They went the chance crate route that most free-to-play games go for.  Its great for Freejam since they can rake in the cash, but the player gets shafted.  Sure... sometimes you might get a very nice part, but the majority of the time you're wasting hours of your life for regular basic blocks and one-off low to mid tier parts that you can't even use since you need ~4 to 12 of any part to actually use it.
The game isn't even pay-to-win.  Paying will only give you a chance to get things as you can't buy parts and things outright... just chance crates.  You'd be more productive throwing your money out the window of your car as you drive around town.  There have been people who bought hundreds of chance crates, at ~$100, and in return they got heaps of randomly chosen junk and not even enough junk to make a fully functional junk bot.
The game is especially crippling to new players now as they have no actual way to progress in a way that will allow them to be competitive.  Since they are entirely at the mercy of random chance they can't really even persue the parts they want for their bot ideas or even the kinds of parts they'll need to be competitive.  The only people who are still "okay" in the current state of the game are veteran players who have massive stockpiles of parts built up.  Which further makes it impossible for new players since they'll primarily be pitted against highly optimized end-game competitive bots.  As the playerbase dwindles the already poor matchmaker will just make things even more skewed against new players.
Its really sad to see it turn out this way, but I doubt Freejam will change their minds on the chance crates as they are too profitable by playing on peoples addictive qualities and hooking kids on gambling in a way that appears innocent.
The game had so much potentially, but they turned it into a casino slot machine and the only ones hitting the jackpot are Freejam.

Age of Empires 2, what can you say more? It's probably one of the most remarkable Strategy Games of all times. It's an evergreen.
So to anyone that is wondering if this HD version is worth giving a try, I want to give my personal impressions.
Altough the launch of the game in April had major flaws. the developers have done things right and the game is finely playable.
The game has one strenght, and it converts into the HD version the same as the original one: this game is one of the best well aged games ever made. Altough it's 14 years old, it doesnt play like this. It still has a very appealing look, while other games that are even younger, like C&C Generals look like crap compared to it.
Basically it is the absolute same game as the titel you may have experienced in 1999, which is a good thing. The graphics and engine is updated so it runs smoothly and looks decently on newer machines and wide-screen resolution.
So many people keep getting this wrong: HD does not mean better graphics, I have seen a lot of people buying this game and complaining in the steam forum s that the graphics don't look better, or aren't HD. Harsh words, but these people are clueless idiots. HD does not mean better graphic. HD is a resoluiton it's widescreen 16:9 1920x1080p. HD ready is 1280x720p.
Nevertheless the graphic looks smoother, and there are a lot of mods out there you can download via the steam workshop which gives you plenty of room to change the appearance of your game just as you want.
The big thing about the HD Version is, it revived Age of Emprires 2 for multiplayer, you can now easily play this game online again. Which is a great thing. I go as far as that this game is still the second best choice around if you want to play an RTS. The first would be Starcraft 2, which is a big thing for a game that old.
Age of Empires 2 still is awesome. And altough the newly released addon isn't an AAA production, which game can claim it got a new Addon 14 years later?
If you get your hands on it, in a sale which is 5 $ or 4 something € get it, it is still awesome.

I've spent around 1,200 hours on this game (I have accounts that do not go through Steam). 1,200 hours is a very long time. I remember each platoon I was in. I made so many friends over the last year on this game, but after each update, some of my friends would leave out of boredom or not agreeing with the Devs. I was always sad when they left, but since I still liked the game I would stay and make new friends.
Fast forward to the Maximum Loadout update. I thought the game was at its best. You could make whatever you wanted, a giant helicopter that could both damage or heal, a frontline tank that could take more damage than anyone else, or even a stealth bomber to sneak behind the other team. No matter what you were, you felt useful to the team and could fill multiples roles for your team.
I was having so much fun with my platoon, expirimenting with different loadouts and trying random builds and seeing how they worked. I could spend hours building an amazing robot and then use it in battle, perfect its flaws, and do whatever I wanted.
It was around that update when I reach Protonium 5, the highest league rank in the game. Admitidly, after playing for so long, I was getting bored with the game. I could at least enjoy playing the game with my high quality robots and my friends. (Probably 800 of those hours were with the same platoons, the same friends).
And now, with this latest update, I find that I am the platoon member who is leaving. I am the friend that disagrees with the Devs. I can't help but feel bad about leaving my friends, but the game isnt what it used to be. I can't enjoy it. You could spend hours making something to have it beaten by 10 blocks with a hover and a flak cannon. There isn't any joy left in the game.
I loved how the game used to be, like a boyhood dream of building with legos then fighting with them, but now its like my dad (Freejam), who owns the legos (my robots), just crushed all of my creations and the time I put into them.
If the game was like it was before, I would overwhelmingly recomend it, but as of its current state, do yourself a favor and don't play it.

The big thing about the HD Version is, it revived Age of Emprires 2 for multiplayer, you can now easily play this game online again. Which is a great thing. I go as far as that this game is still the second best choice around if you want to play an RTS. The first would be Starcraft 2, which is a big thing for a game that old.
Age of Empires 2 still is awesome. And altough the newly released addon isn't an AAA production, which game can claim it got a new Addon 14 years later?

This game is a cult classic among PC gamers alike, and for good reason.
It did not deviate much from the formula of Portal, added a new, cooperative gamemode with an entirely new storyline on the side, and improved upon every single aspect of the game apart from the options menu, which is slightly lacking.
Graphically this game still looks decent after 5 years. It isn't as gorgeous as The Witcher III on ultra, but it'll do. The soundtrack is glorious and filled with fitting music, and the control scheme works perfectly like in all VALVe games.
The story is well put-together and has brilliant voice acting from the amazing Stephen Merchant and Ellen Mclain. The chemistry between the characters, the player, and eachother makes for one of the best and funny stories I have ever seen.
Gameplaywise it's the same as in Portal, but with added puzzle mechanics like lasers, gels, faith plates, funnels. no more high-energy pellets and more. It expands on what Portal did, but by adding in a few of the levels of the first portal, also teaches players new to the franchise how the game works. The puzzles never get stale because of the amount of chemistry the character interaction brings along, and finishing a puzzle to hear GLaDOS being a cynical ♥♥♥♥♥ to you again really feels like a great reward.
If you liked Portal, you'll like this game. If not, you should probably stay away.

When the unstable developers finally decide what game they're actually making, I will replay that game and revise this review.
Until then, I have to give it a poor rating with a heavy heart.
BEFORE: I used to love this game. You would build a robot and then figure out how to engineer it to fly properly and fight in it. In the more advanced stages, you had to build a robot that 'degraded gracefully', so you could still halfway fight and fly when you were just limping around. Matches were quick and straightforward, progression was easy to understand. Fight things, earn currency, use that to buy better bits. This would have been a positive review. I knew how to play it, I knew what was expected of me, I knew what to do to make my game more enjoyable. It was a good game.
NOW: I have no idea what the scrap is going on anymore.
- Your robots 'level up' as a match progresses (???) because this is League of Legends I guess. Except you don't gain more abilities, you just gain more levels. Which invisibly improves how your robot fights. Which is not dependant on how you DESIGNED that robot, it's just based on how well you're doing in that match. Which is, again, invisible. That poorly-made robot you see before you might have 3 levels on you and thus be 'better'. It's bizarre and I don't understand why it's there. Again: Levels don't give you more abilities, or let you 'build' some kind of tree as you fight. You just grind a meter. For reasons.
- You no longer earn currency to buy new parts. Instead, you get 'random' parts you probably don't need. You can resell them, I guess? You aren't told how much they're worth when you get them, so it's impossible to know if what you've earned is even worth the time you just spent. I used to have a ton of currency, but now I have significantly less than I did when I started. They took it away. I guess they 'balanced' this or something (???) by removing a bunch of what I'd earned (??????) but it really just means I can't afford anything anymore. I can't buy the parts I need to make the robot I want, and I can't earn the currency needed to fix this. I just have to pray I get a halfway-decent part among the random smattering of blocks I earn, and then hope it's worth the time I spent earning it. You only earn 3-4 per match and I actually am not even sure where you sell them. It's unnecessarily obtuse. It's weird. It adds unnecessary steps to gaining what I actually want. It's a CHORE.
- There are super-weapons. There are weapons that kill your well-designed robot in 1-2 shots. What is the counter to this? Buying those same super-weapons, which cost as much as an entire robot in currency just to buy one. Many robot have no armor or movement at all, and just one or two of this or that super-weapon. What just happened, what just killed me and where were they shooting from? Oh, it's that fat gun-thingy. How do I get it so I can be like them? Oh, I grind for weeks. Their design looks stupid, but that's OK, because they have a giant gun. ...oh.
- None of my old designs work anymore. Half my garages glitched out and crashed the game a few patches back, and the only fix was to just delete what was in them. My only remaining robot no longer functioned like it used to due to physics changes. This has left me to buying robots from the 'store', all of which handle like garbage but still have a 4/5 star rating in 'combat'. There is a cluster of three cats with lasers strapped to their heads with 4/5 starts in combat. Who is rating these things? There is no way to tell crappy robots apart from good robots. I paid money for a couple robots and now regret it, because I could have used that money for one of the aformentioned super weapons.
- Gameplay is only balanced if you follow the invisible-to-casual-players meta. Which at the moment, is a robot with one superweapon strapped to the top of one solo mech leg. You hop around and it plays like♥♥♥♥♥♥ but you one-hit-kill everyone else's painstakingly-designed robot. There is no counter to this currently, except to follow suit. There are variations to this, but they don't change the meta. You can just strap your super weapon on top of tank treads. Or strap your super-weapon on top of wheels. Or hover blades. Or maybe your super weapon also has smaller weapons on the side. Do the developers even play this game the way I have to..?
- The developers want you to spend money to gain in-game perks, except they (apparently!?!?) remove these at random (garage slots are now free, I guess..?) and nothing you spend money on is guarenteed to still be there when you log back in a month later. The robot you devoted time to build won't function the way it used to. The weapons you spent weeks grinding for will be outmodeled by the latest super-weapon.
What the scrap is this game supposed to be?
- The developers want League of Legends leveling-and-gameplay without any of the balancing associated.
- The developers want Hearthstone get-random-parts-and-pray-they're-the-right-ones pack-opening gambling-addiction progression. Except you don't need 'two' of a card to be able to play it. You need fourty cubes, two legs, eight weapons that match up, left-and-right electroplates in the right sizes and types, etc. A good card drop in Hearthstone gets you 1/30th closer to your desired deck, ignoring that most decks use a lot of class cards and it's thus more like 1/20th. A good Robotcraft drop gets you 1/200th closer to your ideal robot, maybe. I guess. It's painful rather than rewarding. It's actually AGGRIVATING.
- The developers want Call of Duty (I guess?) and added self-healing that completely re-builds your robot if you don't take damage for 4-5 seconds. I genuinely don't know why it was added or what value it gives the gameplay. You could cripple a robot before, but not now, because they'll just self-heal. Not that it terribly matters, because any halfway-decent super-weapon one-legged robot will destroy you in far less time than that.
I have no idea what game the developers are making anymore, and I don't think they do either. I'm getting off this ride.

It's been about a year since I wrote the original review. Somehow just about everything changed and I still have the same gripes with the game I had back then as now. Balance issues persist, drones still reign supreme over all other bot types, and matches still feature people who routinely disconnect and other network issues. Meanwhile the main initiative Freejam has taken on improving their game is to advance Robocraft into 'Beta' which apparently entails throwing everything relating to game modes out the window and changing the point of the game from destroying enemy bots to standing on rings, blasting crystals, and endlessly punishing bots with slow mobility. What's funny is that in the face of all that, they only slightly tweaked a few balance points about the more broken weapons and mobilities to be less outstanding (and to their credit, in response to a lot of player feedback over the past several months as well), but the rush and apparent decision to enter beta and somehow trash every single map they had developed for the game up until that point just kind of pulled the rug out from under everything and shifted the game balance even more weirdly off center.
There's a ton good about this game - robot construction is flexible and stable enough to let players build in just about any shape or configuration and have a functional fighting machine. A combination of paint and various block shapes allows players to construct bots with legitimately pleasing aesthetics and just really cool shapes. The decisions that players make in setting up their vehicle carry over directly into gameplay as well, with the unexpected structural weaknesses and exposed weapons being prime targets for skilled players to shoot in lieu of 'headshots'. At its core, Robocraft is a game with sophistication and reactive tactics in terms of how to fight with basic marksman weapons, and this is an element of the game that has thankfully survived intact ever since I started playing the game back in 2014 - when there were still cockpits and a weird tech tree. Even with all the new weapons they're trying to push, my favorite guns are the Laser (SMG) and Railgun (Sniper Rifle), which both emphasize careful aiming the most of all weapons. In terms of effectiveness though, Ions (Shotguns) and large Plasmas (Grenade Launchers) currently reign supreme.
With everything I've seen, I simply don't believe that's how Freejam sees their own game. I still cite one of their mislead past decisions that thankfully didn't carry through - a recalculated damage system where it wasn't possible to damage components or immobilize enemies aside from just stripping off their whole chassis and vaporizing the whole bot. That was a decision that, if it had actually gone through, would've killed one of the main redeeming factors of its gameplay for me. Reflecting on it, it really illustrates what I think I've come to realize, and it's that Freejam just doesn't know what they want from their game, and still cannot recognize what they're trying to go for. It has no mission statement. Instead, they are mostly trying to blindly follow the leader and seem to be focusing a lot of their attention on making the game more 'accessible' to a wider demographic. That really could just be what Robocraft is, though. They might've just sat down one day and said 'what if we combined Minecraft with World of Tanks?' and somehow it worked for about 2 years. With how much I do like the game's potential, though, I really hope this isn't the case.

A fine sequel to the classic puzzle game. A must-play not only for Portal fans.
+ Compelling plot
+ Humour
+ Setting
+ Great campaigns (SP and co-op)
+ Game mechanics
+ Characters
+ Soundtrack
+ Challenging but not frustrating
+ Well optimised (can be ran on a potato)
- It may take a few moments before things get really interesting
Portal 2 is a unique game developed by Valve. It has a science-fiction vibe and is centred around solving riddles. The female protagonist is brought back to the Aperture Science facility and meets a friendly AI called Wheatley. Wheatley will guide the player through the early stages. After that, the players will get to the core of the game.
Testing – this word is repeated a dozen times throughout the course of action. The player will have to solve many puzzles to finish the game. The riddles are challenging enough to keep one entertained for hours. They are well-designed and should not cause irritation. Moreover, I have not encountered any gamebreaking bugs.
One might ask, is there anything else apart from endless testing? Well, there is. First, a compelling plot. The story is delivered in a linear and enthralling manner. Its tone is sarcastic overall, with an abundance of witty jokes. Secondly, the characters one will meet on the journey are excellent. The voice acting is outstanding. Lastly, the ambience. The graphic style, the locations, the sounds – they all add up to the memorable experience.
To sum up, Portal 2 is a fascinating game that may appeal not only to puzzle game enthusiasts, but just about anyone. Although I found the plot being delivered a bit too slow at some point (due to the seemingly endless testing), I strongly recommend it to everyone.

The only downside is multiplayer with AI. The AI can create major lag issues, causing periodic pauses, ruining the climax of a game. Players end up going out of sync with one another, and cussing ensues.
Overall, with a few bugs to fix up as time goes by, this is the typical Age of Empires II, which should take no time in readjusting to if you've played it pre-steam.

It's an old classic which has been reintroduced for multiplayer capabilities over steam.
It has not changed any gameplay mechanics (for the most part), nor has the graphics been modernized. It remains as the nostalgic - king of the ages, Age of Kings, game.
I have not really experienced the Single Player aspect, but I suspect that gameplay would flow as smoothly, if not smoother, than multiplayer.
For multiplayer, I have only played with friends, and the pings can be somewhat ridiculous - instead of the typical ~50ms, we sometimes connect to each other with ~300ms. However this is managable and you barely notice it once the game begins.
The only downside is multiplayer with AI. The AI can create major lag issues, causing periodic pauses, ruining the climax of a game. Players end up going out of sync with one another, and cussing ensues.
Overall, with a few bugs to fix up as time goes by, this is the typical Age of Empires II, which should take no time in readjusting to if you've played it pre-steam.
Rating - 9/10

I want to preface this review by saying Robocraft used to be a good game. Combat was fun, building was fun, and your performance was influenced greatly by your skill. To an extent, it still is fun. Fighting is still fun, and so is building. But what's wrong now is progression and rewards.
Before the latest update (Epic Loot) there was an RP correction patch. RP is the currency you used to by parts. Players were earning too much in certain gamemodes, and not enough in others. They were made equal, however this was still a giant difference between old and new RP rewards. This extended the time it took to buy certain end game items by hours. If you sold a part, you received exactly half the amount of RP you used to buy it.
Here is the bad part: Random Rewards. As you can probably tell, RP provided an easy way to predict when you could afford a part. Robots often need four to twelve of the same piece to function correctly. Building robots was easy and fun, it didn't take long for you to slap that shiny new Anti-Air Cannon on your robot.
Now you don't get RP by playing. Instead you get a crate. This crate's probabilities of getting a better item are so small, you shouldn't even try. These crates do not factor in time played or the score you get, or any other thing you do in battle. It only cares about leader board position and wether you won or not. Parts you don't want can be sold (recycled) for a set value.
Crates based on leader board position is a terrible idea. Currently, everyone is fighting against their own teammates for that shiny purple crate. Killstealing, and tower stealing are extremely popular tactics. However the problem has gotten better with armorgeddon, as all crates are boosted two rarity levels, meaning many people can get the purple (protonium) crate.
For some reason, sell back prices (recycle rates) for parts was greatly reduced. IIRC, there was nothing in the patch notes for Epic Loot that this would happen. Recycle rates for the cheapest block fell from 50% to 10%. The highest recycle rate for any item is IIRC 33%. This is a massive artificial extension of the time needed to complete a robot.
The second worst part about this update is we have not received a reason why Epic Loot was delivered to us. Freejam is giving the illusion of communicating with their player base, by making polls for which QoL (Quality of Life) features we want implemented first. Mark, Lead designer and CEO of Freejam released an article on
, titled "State of the game, May 2016" Mark says he doesn't want to implement one of the changes suggested by the community: put currency in crates. He says they won't do this because he doesn't want a currency based economy. My question to him is "Why?"
Freejam's community manager reads almost all threads on the forums. At least he says he does. He doesn't always answer them. You can't expect one guy to give an answer to hundreds of threads a day, can you? He does respond to some of them, but he never responds to many threads asking why Epic Loot was made, or suggesting solutions to the problems.
Mark also didn't address any other solutions to the problem. Many of which are extremely easy to implement. One solution being to raise recycle rates of all parts to 50%. No response.
You could say that Epic Loot was the straw that broke the camel's back. Me being the camel, breaking meaning me writing this review. There have been many terrible updates before this one, Team Orders, and Robocraft: Unleashed are good examples.
Another problem with Freejam is that they seem to think we will stop playing the game after we get to Level 150 and have a robot we have completed. This couldn't be more false. If the game is interesting, we will continue playing.
Honestly, don't expect this game to get better. Freejam has never completely reverted a major update, only one small feature; Friendly fire. We don't even need a complete reversion, we just need to buff recycle rates. I've never written a steam review before, I have trouble writing essays. Just let it all flow out I guess.
Even though I only have a little over 100 hours, I've played this game since October 5, 2014.
To Mark, CEO of Freejam:
"Why did you think loot crates and random rewards for doing well were good for this game? What was wrong with currency? Why do you think we progressed too fast in the past?"
I want this game to succeed. It used to be great, the best game I've ever played! I want this game to be like that. Way back in October, 2014, the game was perfect. The core gameplay was decided on. It made sense. Regular content updates like weapons, movement parts, and most of all, maps would be enough to keep me interested. I'm sorry, I just can't recommend this game to someone without them also writing an angry review and uninstalling too.
If you see me in-game, I'm likely grinding.

Mark also didn't address any other solutions to the problem. Many of which are extremely easy to implement. One solution being to raise recycle rates of all parts to 50%. No response.
You could say that Epic Loot was the straw that broke the camel's back. Me being the camel, breaking meaning me writing this review. There have been many terrible updates before this one, Team Orders, and Robocraft: Unleashed are good examples.
Another problem with Freejam is that they seem to think we will stop playing the game after we get to Level 150 and have a robot we have completed. This couldn't be more false. If the game is interesting, we will continue playing.
Honestly, don't expect this game to get better. Freejam has never completely reverted a major update, only one small feature; Friendly fire. To Mark, CEO of Freejam:
"Why did you think loot crates and random rewards for doing well were good for this game? What was wrong with currency? Why do you think we progressed too fast in the past?"

UPDATE:  The devs have clearly put in some effort to address the concerns of the community. In battles, you can now win large amounts of robobits (the in-game currency) such that it is once again viable to progress without having to pay-to-win. Also, they've created more weapons to fill the gaps between average and amazing ones. There's always something affordable.
I still feel that the game needs to give you a better picture of what the next level-up will bring. It's not really clear. The old unlock tree is clearly not where they want to go, but the levels have to mean something, or else why are they there.  In any case, it's a fun game once again, and one doesn't feel stuck anymore. The crates still seem to give mediocre items, and this needs to be addressed, but at least with robobit payouts you can afford to buy what you want.
I try to be balanced and unemotional when reviewing games. When I first started playing robocraft, it was fantastic. There was good progression, each battle rewarded you in accordance with your performance, and you could be very creative with your builds.This was because you could buy whatever you needed either with in-game currency from good performance or with cash it the mood struck you. There was no pressure to buy, and premium was so inexpensive that I didn't blink an eye at paying for it each day I actually played Robocraft.
Then all that changed. Now the game is a diceroll. I have received top score protonium crates dozens of times only to be handed cosmetic and useless items. The items are just as useless to sell, and so unless the dice smile upon you, your performance and rank are meaningless and you remain stuck with the equipement you have. It is a testament to the crappiness of this update that most of the equipment on my robot predates the update. I haven't been able to get anything better.
Constant messages are released by the developper about how they're ensuring better quality items are dropped. They're clearly not trying very hard as the stream of sewage (green "uncommon" items) continues. It is becoming hard to view this as anything other than a pay-to-win cash grab.
I'm trying to hang in there, but I'm nearly done with it.  If you're just discovering Robocraft now, I'm sorry to have to tell you that you missed something really great. It's gone now. I'd move on.

Age of Empires contains a perfect balancing of micro-management that's easy to learn and a fun challenge to master. It's a four resource game using Wood, Food, Stone, and Gold to build units and research technologies. Villager AI make resources easy to gather with automatic collection after building a resource collection site (ex. build a mine near gold/stone and they gather the nearby gold/stone without command) . Military is based on a "Rock, Paper, Scissor" system and is explained very well by unit descriptions in game (ex. Pikeman > Cavalry > Swordsman > Pikeman). There are many civilizations each with specialty units and technologies, unique civilization traits, and various access limitations to the primary tech tree. So different civilizations will have varied success to each player based on one's own play style (ex. Huns, which start with max population cap, are great for early game rushing but have difficulty late game against more advanced units since they have very limited tech).

As almost every other person has stated, the new Epic Loot update has crippled the game unless you already have more of every part than you know what to do with. Before the update, you were given an amount of in-game currency dependent on how high your score was, independent of if you were at the top of the leaderboard. Now you get "crates" with random drops and most of the time those drops are either white for common or green for uncommon. There are 8 different items in most crates except for the lowest tier which is only 2, but unless you pay for premium you only get half of those items and the other half of them are there for "incentive." The worst part of it though is you only get 1 of each item unless it is a building block, so to reach your "nominal" counts for maximum dps and redundancy, you have to get very lucky and get the exact same part multiple times. Sure you could trade in some of the parts you don't want for the new currency, except that you only get 1/4 or less (many even down to 1/10th) of the value making it very pointless to trade anything in unless you have 20 of them and you want 2 more of something else in the same tier.
And oh how the reward system got screwed over. Now after a match, you are given a crate based on how far up you are on the leaderboard, but only for the winning team. Only the top person gets the top tier crate, and it filters down from there. If you were the top player on the loosing team, too bad, you get the second to last tier crate like the rest of your team. No matter how well you play, if your team loses, you don't get a good reward. The funny thing is, while they state that the higher the crate tier, the higher the likelyhood you will get better parts, it seems the difference is negligible. You are better off getting many lower tier crates than one top tier, because you can still get anything from uncommon and up in the top tier.
Along with not being able to build anything unless you had the parts pre-update, the new weapons along with the "flattening" made the top tier and new weapons about all that is useable. Unless you get lucky and pull one of the top tier weapons out of a crate, you better be running a lot of rails to deal with the people who have got those items. I say rails because nothing else does enough damage fast enough and in one spot to take out top teir weapons without having to be directly on top of your opponents. You better hope that you get a lot of them as well, because for the lowest tier you need 9 of them to reach nominal count. Speaking of nominal counts and why rails are the only viable non-top tier weapon, some of the other lowest tier weapons have a nominal count of 14! That means you have to make room for 14 individual guns that have to have space to move and can't be blocked. Lets take an example of what you would have to do to get the rail though: if you want a second tier rail setup, you have to get very lucky on your drops 8 times. You won't be able to buy them, because you would have to sell 220 of the lowest tier machine guns to get the 17,600 to make 8 second tier rails.
I joined before the Epic Loot update, and managed to get to level 25 before it happened. I enjoyed the game previously, but since the update I have seen no reason to keep playing, let alone pay for premium! I was lucky and had some tier 1 rails before the update but they are noticeably lacking in firepower. For new palyers I would suggest waiting until they do some serious work on the loot system or decide to change it back.

I used to recommend this game, not anymore.  It used to be a fun unique game where you built your own bot, and that building mattered, and then fight it out in FPS fashion.  In order to appeal to more "casual" players the developers have steered it toward multiple high damage auto-aim guns.  They've intentionally gone out of their way to make building your bot matter very little in how well it does.  You can spend 5 hours carefully constructing  a tank with various layers of ablative armor.  Or you can spend 5 minutes building a rectangle with some auto-aim guns and do just as well.
For many months now, the developers have been ignoring quality feedback from various veterans that have demonstrated a deep understanding of what the game is/was.  Various major Quality of Life fixes that have been sorely needed for months, to literal years go untouched, while they spend time introducing more logic defying, game breaking elements.
And now they've destroyed the in-game econmy.  The old system used to be simple, but effective.  You could earn RP in order to buy the parts you wanted from your battles.  The better you did, the more you were rewarded.  It was a good steady pace where it didn't take an excessive amount of play time to earn what you needed to build your next bot, or buy your next set of parts.  You could speed up this process by buying premium (doubling your RP earnings) or just buying parts with straight money.
That's all gone now.  Prices are roughly equal, but income from playing matches has been slashed an incredible amount.  I can say with no exaggeration that earnings have been slashed by as much as 99.5%.  There is no income anymore.  They wasted who knows how much effort in creating a loot system where no direct cash (RP was turned into robits) is ever given.  "You can recycle the parts you get in crates" they said.  Except recycling rates are now atrocious.  Previously you could sell back items for 50% their full value.  That is now slashed down to 25% to 0.5%.  New players will initially be fooled into thinking this is a good system because rewards are almost completely flat - new or old player, you get roughly the same drops.  And the drops are all random chance.  All the parts for building the biggest bots are now super rare.  Based on screenshots of what other players opening 300 of the highest level crates has shown,  at best you get a 0.4% drop rate for the tier items.
This is a building game.  If you want to build a big laser cannon tank, you need 10-14 of them.  Now you have 0.4% chance to get one per drop spot in a crate (ONLY if you score 1st in the match and your team wins.)  You get 1 slot for a deathmatch game, and 4 for a Battle Arena (doubled with premium.)  If your team loses, even if you outscored everyone else in the match, you only get the lowest level crate.  You're still looking at 50-100 wins to get a single top level item.  But wait, there are many top level items, further reducing the chances you'll even get what you wanted.  This doesn't cover the movement parts for a top level bot either, which are also all just as rare to drop.  These figures are not exaggerations or made up; they come directly from multiple, large result sets provided by players that picked up the 300 crate bundles.   Old veterans with stockpiled resources can build what they want, as RP was just converted directly to robits.  with nearly zero income compared to the previous game economy, this will only last so long.
New players will get gratification early on with the plethora of low to mid level parts to build low to mid level bots.  in a few weeks, they'll start to realize that building a maximum sized bot fully decked out with the parts you want is a pipe dream.  Only the most hardcore players that will literally have to grind for hundreds of hours will be able to build a single high level bot.  The level of grinding required rivals the most difficult to acquire items from an MMO; except usually in an MMO you're going after a single extremely rare item.  Here you need dozens.
The latest statement from the developers is that they are happy with the current economy, putting the final nail in the coffin of what once was pretty balanced and fair.

TLDR: I cannot recommend the game in its current state because of the extreme amount of grind the last update introduced.
This used to be such a great game - build robots from blocks and send them into battle. Sounds fun, right? But the latest loot update ruined everything by changing the "build, drive, fight" formula into "p(l)ay, gamble, grind".
First, the random drop system may work in other games, but it is not well suited for Robocraft. No longer you can buy the parts you want and build what you want. You are now at the mercy of random drops, which is anti-creative.
But most importantly, the amount of grind and / or money required to get the top stuff is now insane. If you are a new player, the loot system may look OK at first, but do not be fooled. Let's do some calculations. Probability of a legendary drop per 8-slot protonium crate is about 1/35. To get most of the high level items from crate drops only, you'd need about 2000 protonium crates. That means either paying 700$ for the crates or winning 4000 matches and finishing 1st in every single one of them if you don't want to spend anything. Assuming you win rate is 50% and you finish 1st 50% of the time, that'd take you about 4000 hours! These numbers are somewhat inflated because you can recycle items. But the recycle rates are abysmal, so the calculations do reflect the magnitude of grind that the update has introduced.
The worst part: despite a massive outcry from the community, the developers act as if nothing happened, calling the update "a success".

This game had potential, but unfortunately the developers elected to slow progression and rework rewards in an attempt to induce compulsory play (read: addiction), and force people to buy hundreds of RNG lottery boxes and a premium subscription... which, to my knowledge, has had the opposite effect.
Unfortunately, the changes didn't just affect the reward system, either - they added several huge, overpowered new weapons, many of which have auto aiming or aim-assist features that drastically reduce the required skill level to score well in matches, as "legendary" items that might drop from the RNG boxes maybe 0.5% of the time, presumably in an effort to keep people hooked. One of the weapons - "AeroFlak" - also functions as a hard counter that renders one of the most interesting types of robot to build and play - aeroplanes, such as interceptors and bombers - largely useless.
They have also publicly stated that they effectively refuse to address either of these problems in any meaningful way.
Even though the community had warned them about it for weeks (ever since the announcements for the changes) through every possible channel.
And even though the community has been suggesting hundreds of viable solutions to the issues created by the new system.
Just look at the recent State of the Game post, and compare that to recent Steam reviews, the
subreddit, the official forums on
, etc., and you get an idea about how much the developers care about what the community thinks of their game and what they want out of it.
I can, unfortunately, no longer recommend this game.

As a newer player to this game and to this genre I've really enjoyed the look and feel of the game.  I can't speak to what has or has not been lost over the past few weeks/months, but as a new player I can say the following:
PROS
-Really enjoy the building system, it could use some more clearly defined hot keys, it took me an embarrassingly long time to realize pressing 'm' mirrored the blocks I was placing.
-Matchmaker seems ok, I've been in a handful of matches where we our team got absolutely destroyed, but I've been in more matches where it was a slog.  I've definitely seen worse Matchmaking.
-You can craft items with blocks you get from recycling unneeded/unwanted parts, or by selling your design on the store.  On the downside crafting is a little expensive.
-3 days of free 'sub' time for linking your email address
CONS
-There is no way to tell if your robot is going to be a non-starter without waiting for the 'Test Robot' stage to load.  Being on a SSD with 32GB of RAM it's fairly quick, but as a new player (not using robot build tutorials) it took me a long time to figure out how to make something fly without being completely out of whack
-I'm not a huge fan of the crate system, it works ... alright ... the opening animations take forever and cannot be skipped.
-You will sometimes get paired up with veterans with high-end items in low-end CPU matches.  It can make for a slaughter
-The game is not server authoritative.  From what I understand the client tells the server if it hit someone or not.
Overall I've enjoyed the game.  It's a refreshing take on the tired FPS model.  Pitting your creations against the creations of others has been a blast.

The most important thing to know for someone looking to maybe get into this game is that it is in Early Access and despite being in this state for quite some time the developers seem to have lost their vision and moved away from their original "Design and Fight" game model to one more conducive to micro-transaction monitization. If you are familiar with the many pay-to-win smartphone games out there, you will find the current Robocraft very familiar.
One big down side of this change is that it cripples the original vision of being able to design creative vehicles. The nature of the random loot rewards means you either have to pay (real money) for large amounts of crates ($100 in crates would be a reasonable initial invenstment) so you can get enough of the same type of parts to even have a hope of designing what you want, or you plan on grinding for months with whatever cobbled together frankenstein of a bot you can manage.
This isn't to say you cannot sell the unwanted parts for in-game currency to buy the parts you want. The problem is the exchange rate is very, very bad with respect to the cost of the parts (10% - 30%). In addition, the random nature of the drops makes it undesireable to exchange any parts, since you never know when you will need one of them to make a design you just thought up ... or more realistically collect enough matching parts to make a complete bot, ignoring if you wanted to play that type of bot in the first place.
For example: movement types are collected one at a time, and you usually need at least 4 to be stable. So you would need to sell 4-5 random movement parts to buy just one of the type you actually wanted. On the other hand, if you kept those movement parts you would be partially along in 2-3 other movment types that you might want to try out later. So you have the choice of sacrificing being able to make multiple bots later for progress on making one bot now. The same goes for weapons, you could sell multiple weapons to buy a single weapon you wanted, but since you need 4-10 weapons per bot you really sacrifice your future ability to create bots if you do that.
In conclusion, the game had a lot of initial promise which seems to have been lost in the developers desire to turn it into a pay-to-win smartphone style game. My recommendation is to skip the Early Access stage of this game and wait for the final release of the game to see what the developers actually end up delivering.

Age of Empires 2 was already my favorite RTS of all time.  Excellent balance between civs, outstanding civ selection, outstanding map and game mode variety, good balance between economy management and combat as well and macro vs micro control.  Controls are tight and system specs are relatively low.  Basically, by virtually any measure of an RTS this game, this game nails it.  Of course the graphics are still relatively dated but the color palette and sprites used are still just fine and rather pleasant to look at.  Even before this reboot, there was a lot to this game, but now there is tons of new, worthwhile content that complements what was already there.  Multiplayer is now easy and worthwhile with matchmaking and an elo system that should put you in the same ballpark as your opponent.  Definitely pick up this edition, the Steam Workshop makes mods a snap.  My only gripes, and they are minor,  multiplayer sometimes lags and there still isn't a "make your own civ" options for singleplayer/non-ranked multiplayer games despite all the development that has gone into it to date.  These things take nothing from what is already here however.  This is a classic in the best sense of the term.  Score 9.6

Well, when I first wrote a review about this game, it was quite a while ago.  I wrote about how fantastic the game was, and how it was one of the best game I have ever played.  Now, things have changed.  I'm not changing from a positive overall review, because the game is still recomendable.  But only just.  So, here is a pros and cons list
Pros
Very unique gameplay
Tons of variations in play styles
Building is pretty quick, and with some trial and error can become super easy
Not too many gamemodes, but more will be added, and they are all pretty fun
You can play with your friends, which is super fun
Very active community, which can be a good and a bad thing
People are usually pretty nice in the chat, and when they aren't they are often told off by other people in the battle
Cons
In-game economy is completely messed up, you can't choose what parts you get, which is a major issue
Advanced tactics are close to unlearnable, and there is currently no tutorial
Chat system is typing, which is fine, but obviously you can't type and move at the same time, which is annoying
Scoring system doesn't make any sence
A new player will progress very quickly at the beginning, but the progress will grind to a halt very quickly after the first few weeks
The AI in single player mode is hysterically terrible
The devs do chat with us, but they don't really seem to realize that the newest update (the one that messed up the economy) has gotten extremely negative reviews.  If you want to know what I'm talking about, just check out the subreddit, or steam.
So, This game used to be a solid 9.5/10 for me.  Now, it has dropped to a 6/10.  I hope the developers begin to realize what they have done to their game, and that it is currently going backwards.  I still think they will, however, so we will see.  My advice is to hold out for a little while if you are considering getting this game.  If they improve it, then it will be, once again, a fantastic game.  If they don't, well, there are other vehicle combat games on the market.

I may not be a super old or veteran player, but I feel entitled, as a paying costumer, to give my opinion about this game.
Bad design choices, bad design choices everywhere. I won't go super detailed as some old veterans, like Juvar23, so I will just quickly comment on why I stopped recommending this game to my friends:
The last update, Epic Loot, was a good idea. But they executed it in a manner that it feels like one of these mobile games with a life spam of 1-year or less, made to extract the biggest amount possible of money.
It's unrewarding, it's relentless, it's not fitting for a game with the premise of BUILDING things. The issue is, the mind behind Freejam, Mark Simmons, is too dellusional over his own work to admit it's flaws, effectively leading the game to disaster.

Here's an "interview" with the developer team which nicely sums up the current robocraft situation:
This used to be a fun game where you got rewarded with ingame currency and access to new robot parts every few hours of playing. Cycle of purchasing set of new parts, building a robot and fighting against others in a team deathmatch or MOBA-style game type was quite fun.
Then Epic Loot update broke the game completely:
- it removed the progression
- it removed the currency
- it added crafting instead of currency, which isn't really a thing since recycling items gives too small fraction and thus no value
- it removed the matchmaking barrier between players, so now Veteran players armed to the teeth with items worth hundreds of thousands of robits now play against robots worth just a few thousand robits. It's called "Seal clubbing".
- it added loot box system - after every game you get a few random items. I now have one spider leg, 1 medium size laser, 14 wings (but no good air weapon), 3 wheels of different type, 1 ski and a robot leg.
I built a new robot every 2-3 days before the patch, now I have done one in two weeks because parts drop one by one instead of in sets, like I used to buy them in the old currency.
Developers say that everything is ok ;)

First I would like to note a few things:
1: I've played this game 251 hours since August 2015, and have seen many game changes.
2: The reason I chose to recommend this game is because it has potential, and I know becase I played before this last major update (Epic Loot), so I know how good it can be if Freejam does a good job. Its still a WORK IN PROGRESS, that being said the game can still turn out to be as fantastic and fun as I remember it being.
3: I will try to keep my opinions and fact seperated, but remember that you may think differently when you experience it for yourself. Take all these reviews with a grain of salt so to speak. It's free to try it out yourself. No harm done to play it and decide for yourself if you want to give it a shot.
4: I am going to ignore bug issues and lag since it is still early access, and it's pretty regularly fixed and patched.
The Things This Game Does Well:
1: The construction and building of Robots is fun, and very easy to use. Being able to build your craft from scratch, block by block, makes victory all the more enjoyable. I've always found it enjoyable to spend time editing my designs, improving them both visually and in preformance. You can make pretty much anything you can think of, from mechs, to racecars, even real life tanks and jets. Yes, even a dragon (I built one). You don't have to be creative with your build either to still be a good player, which brings me to my next point.
2: The game is still very skill based. Just about every build can be viable as top tier, provided you know how to use it well. While you may be a great builder of Robots, if you don't know how to pilot it well, your score will show. The game types are standard and easy to learn (team deathmatch, destroy enemy base, free-for-all), but getting good at them takes a bit of practice. Since you will always be matched with people who have similar levels of equipment and weapons, skill is usually the deciding factor in who wins in a fight. I've seen players have the most basic designs and weapons beat players with well designed builds numerous times.
3: This is a very team based game, and a fun game to play with friends. I spent most of my hours on this game with friends. In fact it makes the game easier to work as a team. Having support and being a team player makes this game much more enjoyable. You don't always have to be the crazy one-man-team to be a good player and get a good score. You can get just as good a score by making somebody else do it, and making sure they stay alive.
Things The Game Should Do Better With
1: The economy of the game has become a mess to say the least. It used to be very simple; you play, get points based on how well you did, and buy the parts you want, then maybe sell old parts you don't want anymore. If you pay real money to get premium for a day, you get twice the money per game that day. You could also pay real money to get any part you wanted if you didn't want to grind and had pocket cash to burn. Now its a random roll after each game to see what parts you get. While getting premium still lets you get twice as many components as normal, you still don't get a choice as to what you get. You also can't buy particular parts with real money anymore, you just buy another high level loot roll and hope what you want is in it. You can still sell your parts to get points to buy the parts you want, but its at 40% or less sell back rate. This can make it very difficult to get the parts you want. This effects old players minimally since we already have everything we want and need, but this hinders new players from being able to get anywhere.
2: This game has always had a hard time finding a way to balance some game mechanics. While this has indeed gotten better over time, some mechanics are just absolutely game breaking. The damage distribution system is one of the major problems, as this can and has caused outbreaks where one design is found to be incredibly unfair, or several have suddenly become completely useless. The developers have addressed them in the past, but it can take a great deal of time in some circumstances, or they do not go far enough in their changes to fully address the problem.
At the end of the day, it's still your pick as to whether or not you will play and enjoy the game or not. I would certainly recommend that if you choose not to play it due to the problems mentioned above, to check back on it after the next few updates and see if you might enjoy it.

What differences five years can make! This game is a lot like the original Portal, except more polished and realistic. It has a proper story in it unlike the first one, and the choice of enemies is certainly interesting. I enjoyed sparring with GLaDOS again
Learning about Aperture's history was also facinating and added depth to the barebones plot of the first game.
Gameplay has been expanded and this has been one of the best parts. Yes, the classic gameplay from the first game is still there (and yes, you can still make holes in reality) but to make it more interesting and worth your money (as opposed to say, if you have played the first game you have also played this one) you have more toys to play with. There are hardlight bridges, allowing you to literally walk on sunshine, various gels with various properties, and aerial plates that fling you up in the air, to name a few things. There are more variations in the envionment as you go through the different versions of Aperture Laboratories/Science. In other words, this is not exactly like the first game, and the puzzles are more changeable.
The only gripe I have is the odd placements of the loading screens from time to time. Sure, having loading screens in lifts makes sense, but sometimes you see it right in the middle of walking. That was a little confusing and it kind of broke the 'flow' a little. Still, minor trouble, nothing special.
All in all this sequel takes all the great stuff from the original, and revamps it as well as adds more mechanics to make it interesting. If you loved the first one, like I did, chances are you will love the second one as well.

One reason for its success was innovative game play.  Portal is a puzzle game masquerading as a first-person shooter. The player wields a “portal gun” which creates shortcuts through physical space: Shoot it at a wall and a glowing “portal” appears at the point of impact. Shoot again in a different spot and it makes a second portal. Now the player can walk right through the first portal, and out the second. Think of it as a teleportation gun that requires the player to shoot surfaces to identify the start and end points of their trip.Valve uses this mechanic in complicated puzzles where the player is required to get from one end of the room to another.Players create portals to jump over obstacles, get around barriers, and even crush enemies, teleporting stuff so it falls on top of them.

Portal 2 is the sequel to the classic game portal, both being first person puzzle games.
The plot of portal 2 is a direct continuation to portal one, so...spoilers. after the end of the first came you are captured and brought back inside the facility, only to be put in stasis. From there, wheatley, a new AI sphere companion, busts you out of your stasis pod and tries to help you escape. From there,♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and spirals out of control.
portal 2's gameplay is more or less exactly the same as the last game. The controls do feel a bit smoother than the last one, and the puzzles are alot more difficult than those in the first. However, throughout portal two new mechanics, such as anti gravity machines, gel's and co-op are introduced. There are two campaigns, one meant entirely for solo play, while the other is meant for co-op only and requires another person to actually enjoy. I only experienced the solo campaign, so i will focus on that.
The solo campaign has all the charm the original had and more, everything from the humor to the creativty of the levels is ramped up drastically. While the original game was extremely funny at times, this one keeps that level of comedy constant throughout the campaign from start to finish. The new levels are also extremely satisfying to play through, like before, each level feels like a reward for beating the last, now with added dialog to make you laugh yourself silly. The plot, while relatively simple when you look at it from a objective standpoint, really is a step up when compared to the original, especially when you realize what is at stake. If you also read into some of the smaller details. this relatively dark humor based game becomes genuinely depressing to, such as the actual reason all the characters actually exist in the first place and just how sad those reasons are. Every bit of dialog exists for a reason, every little clue in the game is worth remembering as it will come into play at some point down the line, even the final boss battle requires you to remember one specific bit of dialog from earlier on in order to actually realize "oh, so thats where i should aim".
This all being said, the game is not without its flaws. Several puzzles later on in the game are really annoying, as very important aspects of said puzzle are hidden in obscure corners of the map and i only stumbled upon them by rage scrolling the mouse frantically. The levels in the old part of the labs are great, but there is more visual clutter, which can distract from the elements of the puzzles. While this does not make any of the puzzles extremely difficult, this does cause minor frustration at times.
The game has seen massive amounts of polish though, visually, the game is stunning, even compared to most modern games. The soundtrack is back with a vengence to, unlike the previous game where it was always there and wonderful, but easy to forget about, portal 2 features a much more noticable, distinct soundtrack with a wider variety of tracks that doesn't distract you from the gameplay unless you actually stop and listen. I was even informed by a friend that
Overall, Portal 2 is everything good from portal two, with more polish and greater variety of gameplay. If you were a fan of the original, you will love this. If you found portal one a bit bland but liked the gameplay, portal two improves on the clean cut graphics and adds in more dialog. If you love puzzle games, get this and the original. Even if you don't like puzzle games, there is still something for you as the puzzles aren't mind-bendingly hard but still difficult enough to make you think.

Robocraft is a game about building your own robot from a huge numbers of part and battle against other robots in a third person style shooter.
As you can see, I spent a long time with the game and really, really liked it. Unfortunately, the direction the developer decided to take isn't mine. In the past, you had a performance based reward system that made it easy to get the parts you need to build a robot.
Now, the reward system is largely based on luck and randomness. Good luck getting all the parts you need to build the robot you want in a timely manner. It's not possible anymore.
In the past, you could spend money to get part that you want. Currently, you can spend money on a lottery-like system (buying crates with random items). This system is proven to work for games like Hearthstone, but in a building game, where you need a certain amount of wheels, tracks or guns, to build the robot you like, this just isn't fair for the player.
Edit: Coming back after more than 12 months, the  above is still valid. I don't see how a new player can get a robot in a reasonable way (without paying too much money or grinding). It doesn't help that the developer still doesn't seem to have a clue about how the game should be balanced. The changes after patches are still huge, with good chances that the robot you built is useless since something was considered too strong, so the heavy-handed approach is to nerf it below anything else, instead of trying more subtle tweaks (you can't expect that after all the time, I guess).

A re-vamping of the classic Age of Empires II (released in 1999), this game offers only cosmetic changes (until you purchase the DLC, and/or mod it up). While the original is a great game, a classic, and will go down in history as one of the greatest RTS' ever made - hell, it revolutionized the entire genre - I only  recommend the updated HD version when it is HEAVILY DISCOUNTED.
Everything is exactly the same, but (at the time of writing this - 8 months after release) the multiplayer still has ENORMOUS lag and latency issues that BREAK THE MULTIPLAYER - a huge part of why people want to play this game: with friends.
It gets my recommendation as I have sunk thousands of hours over the past 14 years into the game, and it boasts a damn near perfect single-player experience, but if you're looking at this as your go-to RTS multiplayer game: look elsewhere until the multiplayer lag issues are addressed.

Age of Empires II is disputably the greatest RTS game ever made. The sheer variety of maps, units, technologies, and playable civilizations make it a force of its own, but the game attains premier status with its incredible map/scenario making tool, a killer campaign, well-balanced gameplay, and generous catering to multiple play-styles. Age of Empires II: HD Edition is not a remake, but merely a rerelease with a few changes, including widescreen support. Neverthless, the release was long overdue, and it is the one of the games I am most happy to have in my Steam collection. Disclaimer: this review is also for "The Forgotten" expansion pack.
* Incredibly huge game with near-perfect gameplay and virtually timeless game mechanics. Many features of newer games are a tad hard to replicate, such as auto-explore,(hold shift to create waypoints then click on your map all over), but the game othwerise stands up to the test of time quite well.
* Units, when grouped together, create tactical formations to your specifications. AOE2 was the first game to do this, and no game has yet done it so well as AOE2.
* Greatly expanded and updated multiplayer options, including the treaty mode which gives a huge advantage for "turtle" players, a population limit of up to 500, and automatic ELO online rankings.
* Steam Workshop support with active modding community, including HD texture packs.
* Online multiplayer has noticeable but acceptable lag.
* The achievements are WALLS of text that do not fit into Steam's mouse-over UI when checking on achievement progress. Here is an example of one of the longer achievements: "Over one hundred of your units were lost in this battle - even with such great losses, if they were well used against the enemy you did the right thing. Get used to studying the battle stats after each match with an opponent - did you have the right complementary mix of units? Did you make your enemy pay for every one of your losses? Every unit sacrificed is an opportunity to learn about your opponent."
* I encountered a potentially serious bug where everyone's name switched to "[unknown]" and we all had to navigate by player-color. Chatting was very difficult.
* The game is not FULLY steam compatible. The F12 key, which should take screenshots for Steam, loads the "save game" menu. This makes taking in-game screen-shots an annoyance.
* No "military drag" feature, which allows you to select a group of units EXCEPT for villagers. This was first introduced in AOE3.
* The game had a horribly messy launch which gave many people a bad first impression. Most bugs and glitches have since been fixed.
* This is a must-buy for anyone who enjoyed the game when it was still in its hey-day. If you have not played it before, you may consider waiting until it is on sale (it is on sale for the worthy price of $14.99 at the time of this writing).

This game has a brilliant premise, and given me a few hundred hours of enjoyment.  You build fighting robots out of armor cubes and stick functional movement and weapon components onto them.  Then you pilot them in a team vs. team environment.  The game plays quite smoothly, and the dynamic damage system lets you tear bots apart piecemeal, adding a level of precision to the combat that sets it above most vehicle shooter games.
Unfortunately, the developers lack any foresight when it comes to balancing, and it's gotten steadily worse with each update.  For example, they've added several highly specialized weapons that excel in certain situations but are highly limited in others.  This would be great if not for a relatively recent decision to allow you to place multiple weapon types on a bot.  The result was that bot diversity immediately plummeted, as everyone can now build bots that have no weaknesses or limitations.
Imagine what Team Fortress 2 would be if the sniper was also issued a rocket launcher and flamethrower, and that's the current state of Robocraft.  Sadly, the developers seem perpetually oblivious to the harm they're doing to their game, and every update over the past year has taken it from a brilliant class-based team shooter with an extra addition of clever robot engineering, and turned it into a unique but mediocre shooter with robots that are functionally indistinguishable.
I'll definitely be paying attention to it's continued development, in the hope that the developers significantly change tack.  Robocraft not only has the potential, but has flat out demonstrated, that it can be one of the best games I've played, but in its current state I wouldn't recommend it.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.
