I have significantly more hours than it says on my account, seeing as I started playing before they connected to steam. I used to GREATLY enjoy this game, sitting back with a few friends and casually playing a few. The newest updates, however, ruined this game for me. It is now legitamately a pay to win game. They added several new blocks that cost $10 or 10 MILLION IN GAME POINTS. These blocks are insanely overpowered, and seeing as they nerfed the amount of points you get in a game to a few thousand, it would take a disgusting amount of time to farm up for them. So while your trying to farm up for these overpowered blocks, your fighting other people who can teleport, create indestructible shields, firing lock on missiles, and shooting flack guns that have a huge range and aoe damage. However, I have a much larger complaint about this game. Quite a while ago, I decided to buy some premium points because I really enjoyed the game and wanted to support the developers. I used these points to purchase some blocks, and was happy with my purchase. With the recent updates they removed almost all of the blocks I had purchased. I did not recieve any sort of refund whatsoever. This is one of the things that really gets to me. They used to have a neat system of tiered armor blocks with increasing health and increasing weight. This allowed interesting interactions while creating robots, such as the fact you had to use lower tier if you wanted to build a flyer, or having a core of higher tier armor. They removed all of those and substituted it with one block. Simplifying a game whose focus is on creativity and building is a poor choice, in my opinion. They also SIGNIFICANTLY simplified the tech tree, making it completely linear and removing any sense of agency in your ascesnion of the game. Overall, I would not recommend this game to anyone.

The original Portal had the element of surprise. Its style of first-person physics-based puzzle gameplay was unique. GLaDOS, the murderous robotic villain, was new and vibrant and evil in the most charming way. Cake jokes and songs about surviving dismemberment were still hilarious. It was short, succinct and essential. Creating a sequel without playing all the same notes and making it feel like Portal: The Longer Version is a tough task. For Valve, it's apparently no problem.
From the first moments of waking up in the rusting Aperture Science facility to right before the credits roll, Portal 2 rarely falters. The world is bigger, the story thicker, and the character development more surprising. The mania of GLaDOS, the facility's operator, is molded into unexpected forms alongside a host of brutally funny personalities. The history of the Aperture Science facility is filled in, character origins discussed, and though its pacing suffers as it occasionally strikes a more serious tone, an abundance of cruel jokes and cheerfully sincere death threats prevent it from losing its sarcastic charm. When you're not staring at your screen with wrinkled, pained expression on your face trying to figure out a puzzle, expect to be laughing.
You still play as Chell, dragged back into Aperture after the events of the first game. You soon meet Wheatley, a spherical robot, voiced by Stephen Merchant (The Ricky Gervais Show, Extras) who helps you through the early stages. It's difficult to overstate how Merchant's obvious enthusiasm for the role benefits the game. No word Wheatley speaks is without witty inflection, and the consistently clever writing perfectly complements the onscreen action. It's easy to be be just as concerned about missing lines of dialogue as about progressing through the puzzles, especially during Wheatley and GLaDOS' verbal sparring matches.
The attention to detail throughout is nothing short of stunning. The facility is in a state of disrepair at the beginning. Once GLaDOS whirs into action, so does the facility, becoming an extension of her body and personality. When you enter a room mechanized crane arms and wall plates spin and shift with an urgency like you walked in on them with their pants down. As Portal 2 progresses, the environments expand from claustrophobic test chambers to yawning underground chasms. Metal girders and structural supports break and crash into each another, snapping apart in chaotic and natural ways, consistently serving not only to entertain the eye but to expand our understanding of the game's characters. The core appeal of something like Portal will never be the visuals, but it's still impressive how much mileage Valve is getting out of its Source technology first used for Half-Life 2 in 2004.
Though there's a much bigger emphasis on story and character development in Portal 2, you'll spend a lot of time tangling with spatial reasoning puzzles in test chambers. Valve brings back the same portal gun while greatly expanding the number of gameplay toys. The gun shoots two linked portals through which you and objects can pass and momentum is maintained. To get from one test chamber to the next and through the guts of Aperture's vastness, you'll use your portals to redirect energy beams, coat surfaces with globular gel that makes you bounce or run at high speeds, pass over gaping pits with bridges of light and manipulate cylindrical tractor beams. Arriving at a solution will require quick reactions just as often as clear thinking, as portals sometimes need to be repositioned while soaring through the air or before timers run out. This isn't a first person-shooter in the traditional sense, but at times it can feel like one as you zoom in with your portal gun to spy distant targets and frantically adjust your aim and fire with precision.
As good as the single-player story is, the co-operative is the real highlight of Portal 2. The beginning of the co-op picks up right after the end of the single-player game, giving you and your partner control of two robots, and serves as a continuation of the story of Aperture Science. It features fewer characters than the single-player mode but is still filled with enough sharp writing, deadpan jokes and absurd humor to keep you entertained between puzzle sections and provide motivation toward an end goal. Better yet, instead of simply recycling puzzle designs from the single-player portion, the inclusion of another player significantly alters the way you need to think.
That's because each of the robotic co-operative characters carries a portal gun, which means two guns and four portals. Valve takes full advantage of the increased capacity for dimensional holes by raising the level of challenge and coordination required. As is obvious if you've ever played Left 4 Dead, Valve knows how a good co-operative mode requires a game design that doesn't simply encourage but requires you to work together. In Portal 2, communication is vital to success.
Getting through can be frustrating, especially if you're playing with someone you don't know, because there's no diffusion of responsibility here. You can't hide in a corner and wait for someone else to do all the work. The contributions of each person involved are plain to see, and Valve's developed numerous tools to help make communication as smooth as possible.
You can set context-sensitive markers on parts of the environment to wordlessly indicate where a portal should be placed, where a partner should move, and even trigger a countdown clock to synchronize when switches should be hit or buttons pressed. The indicators may feel superfluous at first, but once you're setting up four portal chains of light bridges to block turret fire or redirecting edgeless safety cubes as they fly through open air over bottomless pits, it's obvious how useful they can be. Barely a moment will go by in silence while playing Portal 2 with another, except when you're listening to GLaDOS belittle your intelligence with endearing sarcasm.
Really the only place Portal 2 falters is in the second act of its single-player mode, where the pacing sags and the story becomes more concerned with the past than anything else. Even so, as compared to many other linear first-person games where the stories are little more than shrink wrap and glorify a blood-is-progress philosophy, Portal 2's mid-game doldrums are relatively far more creative and confidently original. Valve's sequel serves as the anti-Call of Duty. Portal 2 is a first-person thrill ride from beginning to end that challenges you to think without failing to entertain.
The original Portal benefitted from its brevity. It had a concise story paired with inventive first-person puzzle mechanics that challenged you to be creative while pulling the trigger. Portal 2 makes the original look like the prototype it was. It's filled with a larger cast of characters vividly brought to life through brilliant writing and some of the best voice acting in video games. Its puzzles are challenging without being unreasonable, and, once you're finished with the single-player mode, one of the best co-operative experiences on the market awaits.

MULTIPLAYER
when you've completed the singleplayer campaign, you're not even halfway through the game, there are tons of levels yet to explore. together with a friend, you will face many new challenges requirering teamwork and good timing.
Difficulty
The game's difficulty depends on your puzzle solving skills. There is no difficulty or hints, should you get stuck and not be able to proceed, then you will need to turn to the internet. I can understand how one would get stumped in this game, with some of the testing chambers being massive.
Controls
The game uses your standard FPS WASD and mouse controls, but also supports a special razer controller, and Xbox gamepads.
Design & Graphics
The game looks great, it runs well on any modern pc, and the specifications match the performance and graphical output. Really great Graphics for year 2011.
Audio
The game sounds great. the OST is nothing special, but it gets the job done in the game. All explosions and sound effects are fine. The voice acting in this game is also great, and the dialogue can be quite funny.
WORKSHOP Support
thanks to Portal 2's workshop support, everyone who owns the game can make levels very easily and upload them to the workshop for others to play. so if you like the concept of the game but already finished the story, you should definitely check out the workshop.

Started playing this game shortly after it's release on steam, it was awesome in the beginning. I never really played it for hours and days on end like some other games (looking at you Mount and Blade xD ) but it was entertaining nonetheless. A year after release it was doing great still, with fairly regular updates keeping the game fresh. But it did not take long at all for the devs to out of the blue do a double punch to the nutsack to all the veteran players.
I stopped playing for a few months b/c of school and work, and came back when they released the Community Robot Factory. Basically they took the fun out of building a robot, spending hours adjusting and perfecting it between battles, by adding the ability to just buy robots that other people built. It only took 3 days from the release of the CRF for 2/3 of all robots to be one of 5 of the top designs, in every battle. The designs themselves were cool, nothing against them. But when half of the enemy team, at times, were the same design... it just got old really quick.
PREPARE FOR WALLS OF TEXT
But the biggest effect the CRF had... was opening pandoras box. Some of the most OP bot designs required such levels of familiarity with the mechanics of the game that they were incredibly rare to see, and annoying to fight. Naturally, the newer players and ones that were just plain♥♥♥♥♥♥at designing bots flocked to the "best" designs. We're talking the thruster sticks, "death walls", and worst of all the ♥♥♥♥ing annoying "flying bathtubs". Oh god, the flying bathtubs were basiclly a couple of blocks, completely covered with shields, thrusters, and guns. They could fire a couple plasma shots while their shields ate damage, then disappear behind a mountain to let their shields recharge. Well designed and piloted by a skilled player, they were nearly impossible to remove from the sky, even with 5+ players focusing fire on them. Designs such as this were incredibly undalanced, but were also rare enough that they were only a minor irritant when they occured. But the CRF removed the element of skill required to make one, so then EVERYBODY had them. Basically the point I'm getting at is that all imbalances in the game meta came to fruition when the CRF allowed everybody to have every bot type.
For months afterward the game was plagued by imbalances. One patch would way nerf one weapon, then over buff another. Then the patch after that would flip it back to normal. After a while, it must have became clear to the devs that this was failing to solve anything. So rather than coming up with some kind of plan to "overhaul" the game and fix all the bugs and exploits and loopholes in the mechanics, they seem to have decided to make the same fatefull dev play that eventually killed or will kill all F2P modeled games: they went all in. They removed the blocks "tier" system, they nerfed credit earning, they added homing weapons, they removed the freakin' pilot seat so snipers had nothing to shoot at, they even made nearly all block colors available only to premium players. The list COULD go on. But you get the point.
At this point, the game is dead to me. Few of the veteran players still play, none of my friends do. The devs simply focused their efforts on grabbing money from newbie players, and left their long time players and payers high and dry. I'm baffled as to how and why you could take such a great game, and then take such an epic♥♥♥♥♥♥on it. Robocraft is dead, I finally just unistalled it. Such a waste, as the game was shaping up to be something special.
TL;DR  If you are thinking of getting this, I wont tell you its not worth it. A new player may find it to be a lot of fun, but you will probably get exponentially more frustrated the further you delve into it, with the crappy mechanics plateauing in the end tiers.
EDIT: Just scrolled through and read the last 50 or so reviews for this game. Notice how nearly every reviewer points out how the game was great and then they ruined it :(

RoboCraft is a great game I tried it myself and loved it!, its fast paced, action packed and enojoyable for all ages,no blood,no gore (well besides little pixel boxes falling apart),chat can be disabled,creative way for making someones mind think and use their imagination,great family fun game.
You start off with 3 different robot slots to contain your robots you make you also have 470 CPU or so starting out, CPU is the max amount of attachments and size ect the robot can have,you also have the robots rank to determan what kind of robots it will face up to example weapons, defenses ect. You also get 3 premade robots to give you ideas on how to build one what might be a good idea to start out, you can edit them or delete them completely and use the slots to make your own brand new ones with you own ideas!.
Pros.
~So far everything is fantastic!
~Starting out is easy and fun.
~You get just the right amount of CPU when you start out to make a good robot to survive attacks and kill back, I came first in so many base attack and defense matches and laughed my head off like crazy, fun and awesome game!
~Theres community guides out there to help you have ideas on types of robots to build and such.
~The money gain in the game which is RP gain is quite good without premium still if you don't like the grinding and feeling like your gaining something then not your type of game but I love it!, I feel like im acheiving a greater level everytime I earn.
Cons.(None really just changes, things that could be added ect.)
~The reward system for leveling up, could be changed so the tech tree is more accessable and such maybe split into more parts like weapons,propulsion ect, more parts could also be added for more choices, but great choices so far!.
~More help on how to build instead of having to read up online tutorials or guessing the controls, when I first started trying to build I had no clue I had to guess the controls until the popup tutorial text finally came up.
Overall.
Get this game if you enjoy those things I haven't said as much as I would like but I don't want to keep you reading constantly I want to see you in the game increasing the popularity of this game making your desisions on the games progression giving ideas on kool new ways the game could go its early access so the communities ideas can come in handy for the devs to make the game a great one for all!

There are so many negative comments about the recent update....I really have to say though, I ♥♥♥♥ING LOVE IT! It increased frame rates immensely and made the game so much more interesting and easier to build far more practical and awesome looking bots. I prefer there being no pilot now, as I feel the creations I've made are drones with whomever has created their bot is controlling!
Leveling became far easier, I was boosted from level 30 or sdo to 70 and quickly became level 100, well, it felt quick but it was still a pretty large chunk of time; depending on how well I was doing but It took me a little to really learn to properly create my bots.
Sure, some weapons and overall matchmaking needs to be tweaked; however, given that this game has plenty of room to grow and is still in early access...I'd give it a break, it's a blast and their are some definite changes and tweaks to be made, but certainly nothing worthy of completely knocking the game.
Major con: Recent update cut RP (Points to buy robo-pieces) in HALF. I'm a member at the moment due to a sale that they had very recently and at first I was making 800k a match with my daily x2 game making 1.4m easy. Now I'm looking more at 300-400k a match with my doubles being luckily 700-800k :L
This I found to be very disappointing, but I've been able to amass quite an amount in my arsenal so It isn't the biggest deal, but definitely disappointing as I feel it limits creativity to create more bots freely as you have to worry about costs which in turn forces you to have a only a couple or so of bots that you can really finely tune.
Again, I'd still give it a try and it's an easy time sink- at least 30hrs free with plenty of content to come and near endless ability to create!

Sequels often suck. NOT THIS TIME!!!!
Portal 2, as a direct sequel, doesn' change much in the base formula, so the game is still based on a more polished version of the Source Engine, is still a First Person Puzzle game but adds a lot of innovations and elements that grant this sequel the status of "Epic".
After the end of the first Portal we're once again in the Aperture Science Labs, but we're in a different section of the facility and the first thing that can be noticed is that the structures decay and some vocal messages hint that an indefinite but consistent amount of years have passed, and thanks to a Personality Core named Wheatley we try to escape the falling facility. Unfortunately We'll have to pass through the remains of GLaDos, causing her awakening and forcing us to become again Her Guinea Pig. You think this is a spoiler? FOOLS! From here the game will show it's improvement as there actually is a HUGE story plot, with plot twists and revelations that will amaze you room by room making you eager to finish the game to see the end and forgetting I've ever revealed you that (predictable) detail.
The innovations won't stop with just a (GREAT) plot, but the gameplay is incredibly improved as well. You won't have to deal with just portal related riddles, but you will face gels and funnels, where blue gel will make you bounce high, orange will accelerate your walking speed, white will allow you to spawn portal on every tainted surface and funnels are transport streams that will make you float in their direction the moment you cross them. You can't even imagine the combinations of all these elements, no to mention the events in the story.
Level design is improved far beyond the first chapter's standards. There will always be minimalistic design test chambers, but we'll have to walk beyond interspaces, factories, dismantled rooms, and immense areas that will make you wonder how big is this Aperture Science supposed to be. You will end up digging so much that you will end up in one of the very first sections of Aperture Science realized at the time of its founder Cave Johnson.
And here comes another aspect of Portal 2. They went so far with the game that hired English (obviously) Writer and actor Stephen Merchant to voice Wheatley and American (obviously) Actor J.K. Simmons to Voice the 'Murican Cave Johnson... And their accent and characterization is definitely great.
Soundtrack is a greatly appreciated news this time because even though it is subtle and thin during most of the gameplay it has some dynamics so you'll hear little flashes of melody when you're solving parts of puzzles, but most importantly there are more studied melodies especially during scenes or scripts.
The last improvement is the other section of the game... Because portal 2 has a single player campaign... AND a Cooperative campaign. We can invite a friend to play via internet and solve 6 sets of chambers precisely studied for cooperative gameplay.

In my humble opinion this is one of the best games, if not the best game, in my Steam catalogue. It is certainly the one for which I have the most logged hours. If I could give awards to my catalogue, Portal 2 would definitely by up on the podium.
To call the Portal franchise 'great puzzle games' is really selling them short on several fronts. And I'm not just talking about the fact that with "first person puzzler" the Portal franchise invented it's own genre. They did it in a way that makes you wonder why nobody ever thought of doing this before. Sure, the puzzle elements like, well, the portals of course, and the cubes and the buttons and the different kinds of gells may be the most easily recognizable elements of the game, but it is so much more than that. The campaign is absolutely great and mind-blowing. And if you didn't think they could do a much better job after the first Portal game, well then Portal 2 is the evidence. The voice acting is top notch again, as is the soundtrack. The gorgeous environments were some of my favorite parts of the game. The whole combination of things makes it an immersive experience that makes you want to see every bit of the world that they are not showing you.
And, oh yes, the Steam workshop for Portal 2 with loads of user created content is an absolutely valuable addition to the game. I'm not always such an addicted consumer of user created content; most of the times I'm like, eh... I've played the official campaign that was made by people who knew 100% what they were doing AND had the resources, so why would I bother plowing throught the piles of stuff of varying quality that other people made? But the Steam workshop makes it very easy to search and select (for instance) the top rated puzzle chambers of all time, and easily import them into Portal 2 with one click. Some of the top rated ones are actually series of multiple puzzle chambers that really are mini-campaigns in their own right, both in length and in quality. Great respect for those creators, and great thanks to Valve for making it so easily accessible and selectable.
And, oh yeah, another oh yeah, I would almost forget the Coop campaign for 2 players, which is an extremely fun way to enjoy Portal 2, and yet another complete campaign to get you hooked on the game. The two robot characters that you'll be playing together with a friend, Atlas and P-body, and the fun and easy sign-based interaction system that they implemented in the game, will help you communicate to enjoy the game and solve the puzzles together.
This is not a game that you will spend, say 20 hours on and then never touch again. I've spent a total of 200+ hours on this game as of now, and I think I am no more than an average Portal 2 addict. But that's just one of the reasons why this game is an absolute must-have. You HAVE to try it.

I was able to build and test many highly varying types of robots and it seemed that my creativity was the only limit to what I could do. However, since then the team behind the game, Freejam, has reduced RP (ingame currency) gains from matches substantially. I now can't afford to buy new parts unless I grind, game after game, for one piece at a time. I've since hit level 100, hoping that by then they would have reverted to their old model, but it seems like that was a false hope. I now have 1 robot and a few spare parts to experiment with, but not enough to build new robots, unless I want to grind. This inability to build new and creative robots has substantially limited the amount of enjoyment I receive from the game and I cannot recommend the game in its current state to anyone who doesn't love to grind.
TLDR: Can't build new robots because ingame currency awards from matches are negligible.

Sequels often suck. NOT THIS TIME!!!!
Portal 2, as a direct sequel, doesn' change much in the base formula, so the game is still based on a more polished version of the Source Engine, is still a First Person Puzzle game but adds a lot of innovations and elements that grant this sequel the status of "Epic".
After the end of the first Portal we're once again in the Aperture Science Labs, but we're in a different section of the facility and the first thing that can be noticed is that the structures decay and some vocal messages hint that an indefinite but consistent amount of years have passed, and thanks to a Personality Core named Wheatley we try to escape the falling facility. Unfortunately We'll have to pass through the remains of GLaDos, causing her awakening and forcing us to become again Her Guinea Pig. You think this is a spoiler? FOOLS! From here the game will show it's improvement as there actually is a HUGE story plot, with plot twists and revelations that will amaze you room by room making you eager to finish the game to see the end and forgetting I've ever revealed you that (predictable) detail.
The innovations won't stop with just a (GREAT) plot, but the gameplay is incredibly improved as well. You won't have to deal with just portal related riddles, but you will face gels and funnels, where blue gel will make you bounce high, orange will accelerate your walking speed, white will allow you to spawn portal on every tainted surface and funnels are transport streams that will make you float in their direction the moment you cross them. You can't even imagine the combinations of all these elements, no to mention the events in the story.
Level design is improved far beyond the first chapter's standards. There will always be minimalistic design test chambers, but we'll have to walk beyond interspaces, factories, dismantled rooms, and immense areas that will make you wonder how big is this Aperture Science supposed to be. You will end up digging so much that you will end up in one of the very first sections of Aperture Science realized at the time of its founder Cave Johnson.
And here comes another aspect of Portal 2. They went so far with the game that hired English (obviously) Writer and actor Stephen Merchant to voice Wheatley and American (obviously) Actor J.K. Simmons to Voice the 'Murican Cave Johnson... And their accent and characterization is definitely great.
Soundtrack is a greatly appreciated news this time because even though it is subtle and thin during most of the gameplay it has some dynamics so you'll hear little flashes of melody when you're solving parts of puzzles, but most importantly there are more studied melodies especially during scenes or scripts.
The last improvement is the other section of the game... Because portal 2 has a single player campaign... AND a Cooperative campaign. We can invite a friend to play via internet and solve 6 sets of chambers precisely studied for cooperative gameplay.

Robocraft - Build, Drive, Fight.
A rather fitting title for a unique game. Your goal is to build designs and fight with them against players from all around the world, Kind of like a MOBA but with a more cancerous community. Host to many questionable Updates and additions aswell as many interesting game bugs/glitches. While it's been out for a solid 4 Years now it only recently went from Alpha to Beta and while it looks and sounds rather simple on paper it is a really technical game. Employing different building strategies and placing weaponry in the right area can give you the edge in battle.
This game has gone so far since its initial release in 2013 which had it as a simple shooter with a small amount of maps and parts to use into the Robocraft we all know and some hate today with a huge array of parts to choose from, Gamemodes, Clans and progression system. While it isn't the best Indie game out there i will continue to support Freejam in developing this gem of a game and i look forward to seeing how it turns out in years to come, Let's just hope it doesn't take too much of a hit on my wallet like it already has... Portal 2 is Valve's second puzzle game, but not just any puzzle game, as it sees you in the ruins of a testing facility in first person view and soon after picking up a gun... that shoots portals. All the while being talked to by a British robot sphere dude that is kind of a
"maron" (won't spell it right because Steam censors harsh words, which is good) that very much enjoys casual and light conversation, jokes, and
As you progress through the game, you also get to learn more about the history of the facility and you even get to meet up with an old
friend!
As stated, this is a puzzle game. Each room consists of a puzzle, with each puzzle getting progressively difficult. You start off with just your hands, then a one-way portal device, and finally a dual portal device. There is also a co-op mode, which can be played before or after campaign mode (though the story in co-op is a continuation of the story in campaign, so it is best to beat the campaign first), as well as the ability to test your hand at building your own puzzles to share with the world, or try some community made puzzles using the Steam Workshop feature of this game! What fun!
- More music and ambiance
- More campaign
- More comedy
- More achievments
- More post-game in the form of co-op
- Infinite post-game in the form of community made puzzles
- A deeper storyline and deeper lore
- In co-op, customization in the form of cosmetics for your robots
- The co-op customization loadout screen is nearly always broken
- The only way to get cosmetics beyond the unlockable ones (which there is not many of) is by purchasing them
- From what I can remember, there is no in-game chat in co-op
- Some cosmetics are unlocked by owning the hat in Team Fortress 2. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the fact that nearly all the hats you can unlock in Portal 2 by Team Fortress 2 hats can only be obtained by purchasing them on the Steam Market, or trading for them. Luckily, they aren't that rare, which makes this only a nitpick
- Co-op is exclusively with friends. There is no matchmaking or anything, and your friend must own Portal 2 as well
Valve made a pretty interesting game here. A Puzzle and FPS hybrid, and it somehow manages to not botch it up. It's amazing to think that this game is the sequel to a game that was supposed to be a throwaway in Valve's Orange Box bundle, but instead that game became one of the most beloved PC games of all time, and even spawned a bigger and better sequel!... Though, for some reason, something feels lost in transition from Portal to Portal 2. The atmosphere, maybe? It feels less creepy, lonely, and mysterious in Portal 2... Maybe it's just my imagination. Anyways, this game is more quantity, less quality, but still good. It can be boiled down to a jumbo marshmallow that was left outside too long: fluffier, tastier, and more to it, but it feels dry, as if being left out for a time made it lose something.
Great game, puzzles may get boring after a while when you're stuck, but I got through and it has a cool storyline.

This review assumes you already own and have completed
, my review of which can be read
.
Game: Portal 2
Developer and publisher:
Released: 19 April, 2011
Genre: First-Person Puzzler with Comedy
Setting: "At least 50,000 years" after Portal 1, Aperture Science Enrichment Centre, Upper Michigan, U.S.A., Earth
Spoiler-free plot summary: After the events of the Portal 1, you, Chell, find yourself awakening in the mysterious science facility once again. However, at least 50,000 years have passed since you were last conscious, and the facility is now in ruins. Your only hope of escaping it once and for all is to put all of your faith in one of the incompetent robots built to maintain the facility, Wheatley, who also wants to escape.
Full review: Portal 2 is a far superior game than its predecessor. Being a fully fledged game with a unique story, unique humour, new game mechanics, and new environments, Portal 2 makes Portal 1 look like a tech demo.
Portal 2 can take several hours to complete; not just because the game is longer in general, but because the tests are far more varied than Portal 1's, and require longer thought and planning.
There are several new mechanics introduced in Portal 2, such as the Thermal Discouragement Beam which replaces the High Energy Pellet seen in Portal 1, but shares the same basic concept of directing the projectile into its respective "catcher", and Mobility Gels which can either make you jump higher or run faster. When all mixed together, these can make several of the later test chambers far more difficult than the previous ones, which means having to think outside the box (sometimes almost literally). At first, these chambers might seem too hard or impossible to complete, but once you've worked out the solution, the "Aaaaah!" moment makes the struggle (and perhaps frustration) very much worth it.
Unlike Portal 1, Portal 2 doesn't have any advanced or challenge map packs; instead, Portal 2 has a challenge mode, which is a combination of the least portals created and least time taken challenges in the Portal 1 challenge map pack. Also, instead of having just six chambers to be challenged on, you have every single chamber in the main campaign to be challenged on! An online leaderboard is also included in this game mode for those who want to compete with friends.
A new game mode introduced in Portal 2 is the map maker. In a parallel universe, founder and CEO of Aperture Science, Cave Johnson, has developed a multiverse device which can send test subjects into other parallel universes, who can test, and steal, that parallel universe's test chambers. These test chambers are the player-made ones you can download and play from the
. With the right know-how, you can make your own test chambers and upload them onto the Workshop for others to download and play.
Another new game mode introduced is the co-op campaign. Set a few weeks after the events of the single-player campaign, two robots GLaDOS has created (you and a buddy) are tasked with solving tests which are used to train you for upcoming missions GLaDOS has planned. This game mode also includes its own online leaderboard and can also have maps made and uploaded to the Steam Workshop.
As said before, the story and humour of Portal 2 are unique. There are several twists that make you sit on the edge of your seat, and the humour, being incredibly dark, can make you laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off, and make you feel uneasy, or even guilty about it. There are several new environments introduced that weren't seen in Portal 1, such as the behind-the-scenes areas of the test chambers, and the ruins of 20th Century Aperture. And although there is less of a mystery aspect to Portal 2 compared to Portal 1, those with a good eye (and ears) can still find some things you'd find out-of-place, even in Aperture Science.
This game is, no doubt, one of the best games ever made. Do I recommend buying Portal 2? Of course I do! Especially if you like puzzles, or humour, or video-games, or not breathing neurotoxin. For NZD$23.99, I'd wait for a sale for when this game is $17 - $20 before buying it.

REVIEW:
Portal 2 is a stunning puzzle/first-person/story-based/cake-eating sim. So........ heres the low down,
Portal 2 is a sequal to Valves suc·cess·ful (Heh) Portal, Portal 2 greatly expandes on what Portal did, it added a richer storyline, more characters, and new locations, it also added gels to use with your portal gun, and Co-Op mode. In this review we will go over the gameplay, storyline, pros, and lastly cons, lets get started!
1. GAMEPLAY
The gameplay of Portal 2 is extremely fun, you man the character "Chell" in different puzzle situations, all of the gameplay is first person. you have to go through different "Testing floors" avoiding lasers, turrets, laser turrets, deadly falls and deadly falling objects. In the game you use a tool called the portal gun, if you are familiar with Portal you should already know this, what it does is well obviously, it creates portals! The gun creates two different portals in two different locations, this is how you will solve the puzzles. The gameplay starts out easy, but soon progressing you will find yourself wanting to look up Youtube tutorials, I encourage you to not go to Youtube, the feeling you get when you figure out a puzzle makes up for how long it took, it makes you feel like a genius! The worst part of the gameplay for me is the fact that sometimes it feels like you are just doing a puzzle because you want to get to the storyline as soon as possible. Ultimately I think the gameplay for Portal 2 is probably 8/10.
2. STORYLINE
The storyline for Portal 2 has to be good, without a good storyline the player has no motivation to play the game, Portal2's storyline is good, its not so great, but it is good enough. The storyline is interesting but at some points it dips into things like shallow and predictable. The storyline has a very neat twist in the end that I will leave it to you to figure out. The storyline doesn't go much into the unknown past of Chell her childhood mostly remains a mystery, it focuses more on getting her out of the facililty and stopping the evil GLADYS (Her name is something like that). I think that the storyline is worth it but it could have used some work. 7/10.
3. Pros
-Great brain racking fun
-Cake!
-Free cake!
-interesting characters
-Puzzles have more than one way to solve them.
-strange drawings on the wall from ratman
-Great atmosphere! A little creepy and mysterious
-CO-OP
-Great soundtrack
And more!
4. CONS
This is an interesting subject since so many people are always giving it great reviews, I will give you the "Nitty-Gritty"
-Lack of player choice (Can not choose where to go, not open world, can't impact the storyline)
-Can get boring after a while
-Puzzles get repetitive
-Not very much variety
ULTIMATELY I would give this game a 8/10 and I highly suggest you getting this game if you like puzzlers.

If you enjoy a good arena-type game, I mean, yeah it can be fun, but there are a lot of issues, particularly with the community.
There is little to no communication amongst teams, just a bunch of edgy twelve-year-olds trying to MLG their way to being the best of the whole game. Nobody says a word to anyone. Everyone just EXP-hoards, they try to spawn kill at every opportunity, and teams tend to be a bit mismatched. For example, the game will tell you as you wait that it "tries to match you fairly with other robots". However, you can have just joined the game as a new player, and you'll see level 17's with their aircraft and sniper guns, and they'll be more than able to pick you off, which they will simply because they view you to be weak, easy EXP for them. They love to hang around in groups and simply swarm the individual player, and will try their hardest to annoy you (be it by sitting still and picking you off slowly as their fellows deal the bulk of the damage, or strafe in circles around you, or simply fly above you out of your reach as they bomb the hell out of you).
In essence, none of the players really care about each other, they just want to be the best. Even the global chat is full of trolls and spammers on and off. You might get the classic YouTube-comment-section-style argument, but it's mostly just going to be some stuck-up moron trying to refuse the fact that they're wrong.
Regardless of this, there are still fun aspects of the game, such as the concept of building your own machine to your style and specs. Sadly, though, nobody does this. All the MLG twelve-year-olds would prefer to just buy the meta and use it. The shop is something that I think kind of breaks the whole game. Yeah, it's cool to be able to buy a design you like, but at the same time all that anyone uses it for is, again, getting easy access to the meta, because they're brainless and unimaginative like that.
Battle Arena is, in my opinion, really the only game mode worth playing. There will still be kill mongerers, but the main focus isn't on killing the opposite team. Instead, it's a territory control and base seige, meaning there has to be some actual tactics to things rather than just a massive spamfest of snipers or SMGs.
Would I recommend this game to you? No. I wouldn't. Too many MLG twelve-year-olds that try too hard and rage quit when they're bested. You don't have to take my word for it, if you're that determined to go for it.

As of Today ( March 12,2016 ) The game is horribly unbalanced.
The ingame currency system is greatly affected by a unbalanced and unfair reward system ( You actually get penalized for doing well and get pity points for doing poorly or not performing at all ), this was intentional by the devs.  In addition if you play well and are a asset to your team your reward is so lackluster it will literally take many many many months of playing to afford any type of higher end weapon/armor/etc.  Majority of players join matches run to thier slaughter to die quickly , then rejoin a new match to capitalize on pity points because doing well offers little to no benefit.
The matchmaking system is unbalanced really having no rhyme or reason for matching players or robot type. ( Example: You get one team with nothing but flying robots and the other with mainly ground units with little to no offense or defense against the opposing team.
Weapons are still unbalnced usually leading to the slaughter of one team over another and weapon types lead to tons of people camping.  They also continue to add new weapons which compound the problem.
Several multi player battle modes but with the game being in the state it is most are no fun unless you like getting slaughtered because of bad matchmaking courtesy of the ingame matching system, people joing your team with half made robots ( lack of movement/weapon items ), people doing as previously stated running to thier deaths, people leaving at the start of the match either willingly or being dropped by the server without the system replacing lost teamates resulting in one team having more players..
There are very rarely any close matches in any battle mode it's always a one sided battle and if you have bad luck you can go on some serious losing streaks that can last for hours.
Once you get to endgame content it gets worse !  Once you make level 100 ( max level which isnt that hard to achieve and just about right as far as required  time invested)  The game wide glitches and lack of balance really comes to surface.  The disparity between cost of endgame items and rewards for playing are seriously out of whack and darn near impossible to manage unless you have lots and lots and lots of free time to play hours on end for months at a time.
The Developers:  Although they claim to try to balance the game more so then not they release new patches without ever testing them leading to serious issues.  They tend to focus on uneeded or unwanted changes and leave the serious issues unchanged. There has been many many times they have outright lied to the community about things and try to pass the buck when serious issues are brought up.
Ive also noticed  the management team really does a poor job and rarely takes resonsibility for thier half hazard actions and/or poor decisions when called to task by the community.
Almost forgot the hiccups. Once yopu play for more then an estimated 20 min or so you wil start to notice freezing for usually a full second or more which will not go away and will get worse and more frequent unless you close the game completely and restart it. This has been a ongoing issue for some time now and no fix in sight.

The Good:
Amazing concpet of a game and when things are right its absolutely a joy to play. Nothing better then being able to make a creation and go into battle with it.  There are a uncountable amount of combinations and designs a player can build and many many play styles achieveable.  A very cool game and superb concept.
Over all opinion:
With all the issues , severe lack of trust players have towards the folks in charge,  unwilingness for serious issues to be addressed in a timely manner, the habit of ignoring the community when issues arise, the unending mishaps created by poor development and mismanagement, and unwillingness to test patches and new content before implementing them, I would reccomend passing on this game.
In closing:
Amazing concept and if done right this game would be huge but unfortunately the development team is seriously lacking what it requires to make a fully fleshed out, balanced, fun to play game.

Pros:
- Building Bots
Cons:
- Absolut broken matchmaking
- Annoying gameplay
- Broken builds wich mostly are op
- New content only for endgame
- Bad PR
- Development
- Bugs
Building Bots:
Leet concept for a game and a very satisfying feeling when ur bot rolls out and works just the way u want it! Building did got a lot more casual, wich lets normal people build descent bots. But there is still the chance to construct extra ordinary bots, using the different shaped blocks to lead the damage u get to certain areas. Or integrating an emergency vehicle for retreat or what ever your creativity has to offer.
Matchmaking:
The game startet to suck a year ago when an attempt was made to create a 'more fair' matchmaking. Because people cried they get seal clubbed in their Tier. Well, that's what happens if you enter a Tier with minimum req and meet another bot on the battlefield with max req for that tier... Story short. Now all matches have a range of at least 2 Tiers, but mostly it's 6 Tiers. This guarantees the most frustrating outcome for you every 2nd game, beeing the lowest Tier in Battle. Well done!
Gameplay:
Gameplay get's annoying quiet quick. The 6 Maps are all unfair. I can forecast a win/loss by the starting position of my team in 80% of the time. There are 3 Gamemodes DM, TDM and an assault mode, where u have to capture 3 nodes and then destroy enemy HQ. The assaultmode takes around 20 min and the winning team is that one, with the least disconnecters. DM is dominated by small/fast drones wich steal kills, really frustrating. TDM is the most descent mode. Match takes around 5 min.
Builds:
In low Tiers, your precious bot, wich took you 2 hours to build, will get ripped apart by hover drones(1-3 Blocks 4 Hover 2-4 OVERTIER weapons, a 2 min build) named 'your mother'. Middle Tier, you will start rageing about everything that flies. Untill you reach the lvl where you can fly yourself, you are mostly just a frag for some sort of flying robot. In End Tier, you will see the same bots over and over again. Creativity? Shut down. Everyone who want's to rule browses the Shop and buys the exact same Robot...
New Content:

If you like to make Minecraft style robots, this would seem to be the game for you. However, be warned, if you want to do much in the way of pvp, you have to pay to win.

So... what to say... listing pros and cons are probably first.
PROS
__________
++If you can imagine it, you can build it.
++Money isnt too sparce, you get just about 195k per win at Teir 10.
+A decent bot leveling system.
+Real aerodynamics
+Walkers, insects, planes, cars, hovercrafts, helicopters, and I'm sure more, are all ways of moving your creation around the world.
+The developers are changing the game for the better... at the date of 3/10/2016.
+Already better then DOTA2 and TF2... in my opnion
+Good gear is a little challenging to get
+Multiple gun types can now be on one bot, meaning you can have a mortar sniper, if you please. (I please a lot)
CONS
_________
--Updates are a little sparce, and some designs of bots may be broken by said updates.
--Some people AFK while in matchmaking, while this isnt their fault, a system like in smite, how you need to hit accept, would be good.
-Matchmaking is a little unfair AT TIMES. you will be put up aginst higher and lower level bots, but that's a good thing.
-May get a little boring with the money grinds every here and there.
-The pFLOPS (the amount of power you are allowed to use per bot) is a little... overly limited. most of the time the game challenges you to rebuild your bot to get into the limit. this is both good and bad because you wont really be able to al the time.
-The game may crash once in a blue moon. HOWEVER you wont lose much progress building your robot if it does. only matches are the worst times for it to crash.
EXTRA NOTES
______
The aerodynamics are hard to understand sometimes, but very rewarding when you finay get how it works.
You need to build for survival, not style. Only in movies do looks get you anywhere.

Robocraft is not good/fun enough for me to grind 100 hours for one module.
Don't get me wrong, I LIKE robocraft, but I don't LOVE it unconditionally. I've logged 428 hours since the steam launch. I'd estimate about half of it was in the garage. So instead of the megabot and ~8 tier 10 bots I made, I would have made enough money for 2-4 modules with the new reward level.
The real fun of robocraft is on the building side, not the the fighting side. The actual gameplay is the weakest part of this game in my opinion, it's clunky, unbalanced, and the maps are quite uninteresting both visually and from a gameplay perspective.
I get 10-20 hours per week to play games now that I have a job and a family. I could pay2win, but by my paypal log I've already spent $400 on this game (Over the course of 3 years.) I also JUST bought 6 months of premium before these changes went live.
In the old days (Like 6 months ago when I last played) I could make 5-15mil in a couple of hours driving my megabot, that seemed pretty good cause you could build a new tier 10 bot for about that amount, and that was fun. I enjoyed building a new bot every few days.
So I'd like to implore the devs to take a look at what's going on here, I think for me to stick with this I need to make ~500k for an amazing TDM (250k avg) win and ~1mil for an amazing BA win (500k avg.) With premium of course.
In general I've always found the people that can afford to put 100 hours into a game usually can't afford to give that game very much money. You need to look for the sweet spot because people like me with disposable income aren't going to spend it on your game just because you made it more grindy. I spend money on games because they're fun, and because I see potential in them to be great. Unless this issue is resolved swiftly I won't be spending anymore money or time on this game, I have plenty of other games to play.

So.  This game is very interesting topic...
-
ROBOCRAFT
-
Now in order to give a full fair review I will have to first talk about the past versions of this game.
When this game first came out, it was a fresh twist on existing concepts. Mixing the fun and strategies that take place in shooters like World of Tanks, or other FPS's. And the fun of building things, and learning what works what doesn't, and what can be improved apon.
This game would grab your attention by having a feeling of limitless creativity when creating your robots, and would keep it because you would always think of new ways to improve your defences, offenses or mobility, while also trying to maintain a balance between all three.  I would constantlly join games and carefully inspect the effects my improvements made, and just kept improving and tweeking.
Now, that is what the game used to be for me.  However with all the updates that have been slowly coming out. The game has changed drasticlly.  Removing, one by one, the things that made building difficult and thoughtful. Like removing the pilot seat. Or removing the different tier blocks, replacing them with a single type of colorable block.
Not all changes were game changing, some just updated the game graphically and improved performance.
But even so, the game today is very different.
Before; you would worry about weak points, item prices, and balancing your equipment. Now; it's mainly about placing as many guns and shields that you can fit on it.
Finally to my point. The game that robocraft is today, is still okay. It's still fun building machines nowadays, but the goals and struggles behind building them have changed. This game has gotten a lot of heat lately because of the changes. And it is understandable, many veteren players dislike the way it plays now, since it's vastly different. But at the end of the day, robocraft is not a bad game. Its still a mediocre title, worth checking out if you want try out building robots and testing them out.  The game went from being a strategic builder, to an easy to pick up one.
I recommend trying this game out if you have not played it before.
-
Extra
-
For all you other reviewers, remember. Robocraft and the dev team behind it are not the same thing. I think much of this game's bad reviews, should be placed on the dev team, and not the actual game.  They don't really have a clear vision for this game, and that single reason, I beleive, has made this game change so much. If they had a clear view on what they wanted it to be, then it would stay more of the same, but just get better over time with updates. (If done correctly)

I have played tons of games on robocraft.  I have played this game since it was awarded indie game of the year, and might I say props to you for accomplishing that. That said, there are a few things that need to be taken into account:
Balance:
The game is EXTREMELY unbalanced, the auto lock on missiles are very hard to dodge and are expensive(more on this later) and now the timer has been dropped from taking 2.5 seconds to lock on, to 2 seconds. Not only is this devastating but the main weapons of the game: plasma cannons, and plasma lasers have taken some nerfs. Lasers have reduced fire rate and plasma cannons increase power consumption. This creates a huge divide from the premium users that paid money to get the missiles easily and the basic players who can only afford one laser of a high tier.
End game rewards (and money issues in general):
I consider myself to not be at the end game, but close to it. My weapons have gotten quite expensive as of late. To list off a few:
Now, this list wouldn’t be too bad, if the payoff was about 60,000~, 80,000~ with premium users in the game. Now, understandably it is frustrating that the most I can get in a game is 110,000~ with a first win of the day bonus and premium users. So, all in all you are required to play approximately 126.86~ games to acquire 1 lock-on missile launcher, let me emphasis this ONE LOCK-ON MISSILE LAUNCHER, and in order to be any use to your team, you’re going to want to pack at least 2 of them, making the amount of games you need to play skyrocket to 252~. This is unbelievable and give NO incentive whatsoever to grind out the game for the RP.
I can hear it now, how can I play this game if it takes so long to get something. Easy enough, you just have to pay real life money to obtain all of these weapons, problem solved. For translation it costs you 2,300GC for 1 missile launcher, that would approximate putting $2.50(and a little more to get 50 more GC) and to get two of them you need $5.00 for it. Doesn’t seem like a lot, but this is a “FREE TO PLAY GAME” Why then would you make the game free and then choose to make the game SUCH A HUGE GRIND that you cannot even begin to reach end game content without going past a pay wall or dedicating hours upon hours to a game.
Additional premium content:
On a side note, I have noticed that glass now costs GC to purchase, no RP method. The three principles upon which this game is built upon is “build, drive, fight” can you drive? Yes. Can you fight? Yes, now building on the other hand. Building has been limited in the terms of glass. Glass used to be a fun cool block that you can use in your vehicle to have, which is now gone, banished behind pay wall.
Things they did well at:
I will update my review as major parts of the game are tweaked, but at the moment if given the chance to rate the game at its current state, I would give it a 4/10. This game is below average, it can perform meh compared to most free-to-play Minecraft cube copy games. However, the game still needs LARGE improvements before it can be considered a game to play.

All these cool huge scale robot late-game items that you figure out after-the-fact can't be used like the robots you played with up to that point. The Beta update is one of the worst possible changes to robocraft.  Just so darned awful.

No more usefull medics

Back in the day it was so much fun, addictive almost, the feeling you've got when leveling up or getting next tier items was the best, the sense of progress was real. Crates are the devil when  it comes to free to play games, they can enhance the experience, or trash the game. Sadly this is the fate for robocraft if the developers keep their ways of not listening to the community.

Fun fact: People don't like change.
Impressive fact: Freejam, the dev team for this game, are willing to change everything to make the game better.
What does this mean? Well, a lot of people get their panties in a rustle every time there is an update.
Of course mistakes are made, but since I started playing the gameplay seems to have overall improved. If something's balance is way out of wack, it is fixed in a relatively timely manor.
Now for my actual review...
The building: Cubes are your foundation, they are the armor for your bot. But these cubes come in all shapes in sizes so you can make sure that you look good when destroying your enemies. There are 10 basic movement parts, none of which are mutually exclusive, so the chassis alone for your creation has massive opportunity for creativity. You got wheels, tank tracks, hover blades, mech legs, sticky insect legs (that can climb any surface), wings, rockets, helicopter blades, helium and sleds. Want to make a flying car? Straps some wings to your racer and watch it fly. Want to strap a bunch of rockets on a hovercraft? Go for it and do laps around your enemy. Want to make a craft that can latch to any wall and fly away at a moments notice? Put some helicopter blades on your walker and go for it. Then of course there are the weapons. You got slow firing plasma with an AoE, rapid fire SMGs, Rail guns, Flak canons, healing beams, missile launchers and even a melee weapon (Tesla blades). And now with the newest update, you can put any combination of ALL of these weapons on one bot. One final part in building are modules. These devices, once added to your bot, give it an ability of sorts. The first of which teleports you a set distance in front of your crosshairs and the other makes a stationary impenetrable shield in front of you. Both of these on a set cooldown.
That was a lot of stuff, and that is the point. The tools are aplenty, the only thing holding you back is your creativity in putting it all together.
The fighting: As you can tell there are a lot of ways to create a bot. You can be the tank that apray and pray's smg fire. You can be an agile plane that unleashes volleys of plasma on your enemy. You can even be a bunch of rockets thrown together with the melee weapons strapped to the front to try and flank the enemy. But this is not what makes Robocraft so special, it is the damage system that does that. There is no health pool for your bot, each part has its own health and can be taken off piece by piece. Does your enemy's bot have a bunch of arms with guns on them? Then shoot of the arms. Maybe they left their wheels too exposed, shoot them off and cripple your enemy. This simple aspect makes the gameply so much more dynamic, you have to make quick decisions when fighting an enemy that can have massive pay off.
So people can whine all they want about how they liked the game more before X update, but if you are new to the game you don't know what it was like before X update do you? So try it, its free to play for pete's sake. If you can only get an hour of fun out of it, well, that was an hour of fun that did not cost anything.

TL;DR: We had a nice, progressive, fairly balanced game. We now have this.

Sure, it's a puzzle game. You can go on and on about the unique physics, the retro futuristic visuals etc., but it's so much more than that. You gotta hand it to Valve. They are the maestros of PC gaming. This is some powerful stuff, a script with suspenseful storylines, quirky characters and a dark sense of humor. Beautifully executed too, with solid voice works done by pros (like J.K. "not quite my tempo" Simmons). So it feels more like a social political satire, with its mild social commentaries and anarchic sentiments intertwined within the visceral medium of a game. Walking around in this gaint abandoned dystopian facility, you know mankind has done awful things in the name of science. It's an obvious reflection of scientific ethics (you can actually feel this in all of Valve's titles). Sure science is helpful and crucial, without which this game wouldn't be built. But science have yet to solve every problem there is. I'm Chinese, I would say that Chinese schools feels much like an Aperture Laboratory where your whole minute existence is dedicated to various kinds of test. There's tests after tests and more tests for the next 65 years (yo science!). Well this kind of notoriously test-oriented education system is probably pan-asian. Students, lab rats, same difference. (Of course this is a lazy student talking...) And for what purpose? Is science to blame? Where's humanity in this? It's also very reminiscent of the movie Cube series, both aesthetically and thematically. Also you can say Aperture is a comment on the kind of mammoth inefficient government, wasting taxpayer's money on some grandiosely ridiculous projects. Wheatley, the friend who starts as an talkative innocent powerless friend only end up betraying you and starting a tyranny when put in powerful position. Your usual plot twist about human weakness and institutional failure. GlaDOS, the Orwellian omnipresent omniscient AI, forever watching you with "Vital Testing Apparatus", a kind of query into the validity of observational psychological experiments or a jibe at the futility of deciphering the complex human mind? Or it's about the law of quantum mechanics that the "very act of observation changes that which is being observed". GlaDOS is clearly the manifestation of the fundamental human desire of being in control. I mean, does any entity sound like a compulsive control freak? The insinuation is obvious. I am of course speaking from the collective experience of being a Chinese, who lives in a place where long history of centralized totalitarian governing tradition is something we are proud of. Apart from the devil-may-care Cave Johnson, the whole Portal universe is depopulated and apathetic, which is aesthetically refreshing, cruelly objective and existentially nightmarish.

Sure, it's a puzzle game. You can go on and on about the unique physics, the retro futuristic visuals etc., but it's so much more than that. You gotta hand it to Valve. They are the maestros of PC gaming. This is some powerful stuff, a script with suspenseful storylines, quirky characters and a dark sense of humor. Beautifully executed too, with solid voice works done by pros (like J.K. "not quite my tempo" Simmons). So it feels more like a social political satire, with its mild social commentaries and anarchic sentiments intertwined within the visceral medium of a game. Walking around in this gaint abandoned dystopian facility, you know mankind has done awful things in the name of science. It's an obvious reflection of scientific ethics (you can actually feel this in all of Valve's titles). Sure science is helpful and crucial, without which this game wouldn't be built. But science have yet to solve every problem there is. I'm Chinese, I would say that Chinese schools feels much like an Aperture Laboratory where your whole minute existence is dedicated to various kinds of test. There's tests after tests and more tests for the next 65 years (yo science!). Well this kind of notoriously test-oriented education system is probably pan-asian. Students, lab rats, same difference. (Of course this is a lazy student talking...) And for what purpose? Is science to blame? Where's humanity in this? It's also very reminiscent of the movie Cube series, both aesthetically and thematically. Also you can say Aperture is a comment on the kind of mammoth inefficient government, wasting taxpayer's money on some grandiosely ridiculous projects. Wheatley, the friend who starts as an talkative innocent powerless friend only end up betraying you and starting a tyranny when put in powerful position. Your usual plot twist about human weakness and institutional failure. GlaDOS, the Orwellian omnipresent omniscient AI, forever watching you with "Vital Testing Apparatus", a kind of query into the validity of observational psychological experiments or a jibe at the futility of deciphering the complex human mind? Or it's about the law of quantum mechanics that the "very act of observation changes that which is being observed". GlaDOS is clearly the manifestation of the fundamental human desire of being in control. I mean, does any entity sound like a compulsive control freak? The insinuation is obvious. I am of course speaking from the collective experience of being a Chinese, who lives in a place where long history of centralized totalitarian governing tradition is something we are proud of. Apart from the devil-may-care Cave Johnson, the whole Portal universe is depopulated and apathetic, which is aesthetically refreshing, cruelly objective and existentially nightmarish.

old review:
ok, since a few years ago in early beta, my review of this game was pretty critical.
I'm still critical of some of the changes they made in the past year involving the removal of the Boss Mode,
the building Tiers, removal of Pilot seats, and a lack of meaningful development for the longest time.
HOWEVER. In this very latest patch, you can now equip more than 1 type of weapon for your loadout on whatever bot you want to build. YES they fixed the crippling reload time on the railgun. YES there are now anti-air flak cannons and missle pods. YES plasma flyers are not the ONLY way to go anymore....surprisingly, they added enough balance to the game to ...mostly...kinda...sorta... fix that. now you are no longer one type of gun. now you can actually have some variety. congratulations, Robocraft, you now can -almost- step in the same ring as Mechwarrior. Almost.
Still a lot of development to go. However, for where this game is sitting now, I feel I can finally give it a reccomendation. well. almost. I'll get to that.
Personally, I'm still going to be stern about the Boss Mode. That was a very original Idea that drew me into the game to begin with, regardless of building bots and gameplay, being the boss in essentially a raid level fight was something I'd never seen done properly in a game until then. I feel they could try it again, if they could fix the Mega Bots and gear them up a bit more.
Downside: it's still a game of "shoot the guns off first". there's no reason to aim for anything else other than the enemy guns.
your bot, itself, has little meaning without a cpu core / pilot.
after almost over a year, finally some meaningful development and progress has been made.
retracted my reccomendation of this game due to server instability. too many lag spikes during gameplay.
When they start investing money into better servers, without the constant spikes, then I think I could give this a reccomendation.
Still a long way to go. But, they've made some minor progress.

So...Let's talk about robocraft, game about building robots (bots,mechs whatever you call them) and fighting with them.
The building itself is done really nice. You start with 37x37x37 blocks building grid you can later upgrade it to 43x43x43 blocks. Nothing exept space (and crate system, but we will get on this later) limits your imagination so its possible to build silly things like helicopter from one block, four shields and one gun.
In the game you have 10 types of guns to chosse from and 4 modules. You can have in total 5 guns and modules on your robot. For example you can have a sniper with (of course) sniper rifles for long distance, lasers when someone gets close to you,Invisibality module,teleport module and EMP module. But the problem is that some of the guns and modules are underpowered and some overpowerd.
The match making (in my opinion) Is at a very bad state now. Previolusly the match making were about robot ranking, so the better stuff you got, you were matched with better robots. Now its about CPU that your bot takes so you can get matched with players that have small robots with high level guns.
The "Epic Loot" Update introduced Loot crates that you get after matches. This update except it broke the community made obtaing items hard, unrewarding and sometimes unfair. Before the update to get items you had to simply purchuse them for the in-game currency that you were rewarded after the match. Now you have to open crates, they come in 6 rarities: Rusted, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Diamond and Protonium. In them you find randomly generated items from the game. In Protonium crate you get 4 items (8 if you bought premium) with the highest chance of geting "good" items (Mostly you get blocks and uncommon guns). In the rest you find one item (2 if you bought a premium) If you get a item that you dont want (and that will happend a lot) you can scrap it and turn it in to Robits. From Robits you can forge new items. The problem is you get 30% of robits from the items normal cost.
The game at its current state Its not worth downloading because its inblanced, the matchmaking is not wellmade, and the crate system is just awful. Wait for it to exit this state bacause in the core its a fun game and it made its genre popular.

I am gonna get straight to the point: Robocraft is a fine game, to this day I still recommend this game for those wanting to have a good time.  HOWEVER, with it's recent updates (and me as the go to Plasma cannon user); I miss the old way the Plasmas would fire, it was a strategic part of the game.  Railguns are still a thing to face, SMGs are still annoying as ever, less drones to fight (WHICH I AM GRATEFUL), but the Missile Launchers are easy to dodge but they have become the new plasmas with their insane DPS when all missiles hit.  Missile Launchers have become the new thing of the weapons that I can grow to love and hate, though I would rather play Titanfall, because of how you can do in that game.  Another thing I will bring up is in this game is MAP CONTROL, most teams that I have faced just mop the floor with the team I am on because they have the MAP CONTROL, and I know that there is some 10 year old kid that will say that the other team sat outside spawn on Team Arena and made sure they didn't cap a tower because that they are scrubs; THIS GAME ENCOURAGES MAP PRESCENCE, A TEAM THAT CONTROLS THE MAP CAN CONTROL THE ENTIRE GAME; last game I was in, it was like this, however since the other team didn't push their advantage on the fusion core; it lead to that team to lose the game because a come from behind victory.  Thing is, you can only contain a team to a certain extent, before they start to get punished for the long contain of that team that was doing it.
That is all I have to say, I still recommend this game; to a certain degree though, have fun guys
-Zezku the Gaming Celesteon

I figured I should write a brief review since this is one of the few free games that's ever held my interest for so long. So here goes:
I joined just after the hated update that changed the tech tree from a branch-out system to a completely linear progression. Level progression is currently more of a token upgrade system than an actual feature. It serves its purpose of providing some satisfaction when you unlock the parts you've been waiting for, but other than that it's just a hurdle. Worth criticism? Sure. Worth all of these negative reviews? As far as I can tell (keeping in mind that I never played the old version) not at all. The gameplay itself is still extremely fun, and since the developers are very good about avoiding any sort of P2W content, the game is truly free.
You could spend a lot of time analyzing the various updates and the current direction of the game, but I'll give the super-abriged version: they're moving away from a heavily progression-oriented game to a shooter with lots of variety. Meaningful progresion now mainly comes from accruing the money to buy lots of cool expensive parts once you're high level, rather than getting to a high level.
When I joined a few weeks ago there were 5 weapons, and since then they've already added two more. As of tomorrow an update is coming that will add new utility parts (teleportation and placeable shields) as well as allow players to equip multiple types of weapons on a single bot. If the patch delivers everything as promised, I think this will really make the game. Previously there were only a couple of robot archetypes that you would commonly see in the late game, since you could only use one type of weapon per robot. I'm hoping that robot designs will now be far more varied, and that creative builds and strategies will really begin shine.
I've had a ton of fun playing this game and would absolutely reccomend that you try it out. It's not perfect by any means,  but its free and its got devs who are really trying (and generally succeeding, in my opinion) to make the changes that players want to see. Please don't let the negative review stop you from giving it a try.

Well, where shall I start?
PROS:
1. You can make your own robot and customize it.
2. It's free2play.
3. You can run it on a potato.
4. The feeling you get when you rank up.
5. It's not p2w.
6. You don't need to have superior internet.
7. There are great tutorials on YouTube about Robocraft, I recommend to watch to Lathland and R0SEFALL.
NEUTRAL:
1. You need to communicate with your team, this can both be a bad thing (No mic) and a good thing (The game gets more strategic).
CONS:
1. The community can sometimes be toxic.
2. In high ranks, the waiting times can be really long (I sometimes have to wait 30+ minutes for a match of 7 minutes).
3. I mentioned earlier that the game isn't pay2win, it isn't actually, but it's pay2rush, it just speeds the process of levelling up.
4. Teams can sometimes be unbalanced.
CONCLUSION:
Personally, I think that the game both improved and got worse. It got less strategic, because of a update. But on the other side, the physics improved and you can have an great experience if you have a few friends to play this with. I would recommend this game for active players, the game changes things pretty often so you need to be active in order to keep along with the meta (if you care about this).

This is my first review so please don't judge me if I fail to follow the form.
Few years ago my brother and I played this game. When he saw it on winter holiday sale he "made me" buy it for both of us.
I finished single player first and I just love quotes, both Wheatley's and GladOS's. Single player felt longer then first game's and that sudden fall and change of surrounding is great. Cherry on cake is credit song which I only saw on Portal games and  make these games so special.
I also like fun that doing these achievements brings, from throwing yourself into pit to breaking screens that results with some funny Wheatley's quotes.
I think many people will agree with me when I say that co op is equaly good but even more fun the single player.
That is the element of game that I spent most of my in-game time on. Playing standard co op levels seperated into 5 groups of courses (not counting bonus courses) is great way to first learn game basics (in case you didn't play single player) but also to realize how good is your partner (how good reflexes he/she has, how much time is he/she willing to spend thinking, is he/she too stubborn to be played with, can you two understand eachother and how good host he/she is). I can say I played with at least 10 different partners I met online and finding few that I really enjoy playing with was not easy task.
I also love the fact it has option to design your own test chamber and publish it on Steam Workshop pretty easily. Thanks to that you can, while in game, browse for the test chamber that is on your level (to be honest probably everyone after playing standard co op or/and single player for few times gets better on understanding game rules so he/she can solve harder tests more easily), subscribe and play it. There are whole collections of tests, some even with custom graphics and voices used to tell you original story through testing. You can choose from racing test to very complex one that require thinking.

Playing this game you can very easily catch yourself asking how did time pass by so quickly. One of my co op partners and I spent over and hour playing just one test, but I don't regret a second because it was so much fun :).
I am going to finish this with conclusion that this game connects different people which all have one thing in common- they are ready to do some testing :)
I really hope I didn't fail form and this review helped someone decide to buy this game and be satisfied with it like I am.
