After
3500+ hours in Robocraft, what do I have to say?
Here are some points to consider about Robocraft:
But, that's one of the things I love about this game.  The developers are constantly working to improve the game's overall appeal.  Sometimes I like the changes, sometimes I don't.  But in the end, I still play this game more than any other because it is just that fun!  And, things that I detested in the beginning I have eventually come to love.
FreeJam seems to have listened to the community and is putting more energy into things that benefit the health of a thriving community eco-system.  This includes the recent implementation of  in-game clans, events, build competitions, streams, Q&A, interviews with developers and community leaders, a revised forum structure, and additional staff dedicated to working with the community.
Often people who have a negative opinion of this game complain about how this change or that change broke their robot.  Or, that the game isn't the same anymore.  Well, that is probably true.  But, I enjoy the challenge of figuring out how to adapt my bots to each change.
If things always stayed the same, then it would get rather dull...don't you think?  If you remember that this is an Alpha game and that things are going to change...and embrace the change rather than complaining about it ad nauseum...then I think you can enjoy it as much as I.  Which brings me to my next point....
There are a lot of people who complain that FreeJam doesn't listen to the community.  I'll be honest...sometimes it can feel that way.  However, I've seen quite a few ideas that originated with the community become parts of the game.  So they do listen but are fairly selective about what they implement.  It would probably be a bad thing if they implemented every idea that came up.  Let's be honest.  Some of them are pretty bad.
However, there are some areas where FreeJam could prioritize better.  I would like to see:
: With the RoboClans Alpha Update FreeJam has improved the overall functionality of chat and introduced basic clan features.  They have also given a roadmap of their plans to expand these features and their functionality.  A basic tutorial was added in an earlier release, but I'd like to see more work in this area.
There are some bugs that are a bit frustrating.  I personally haven't seen the most obnoxious bugs in quite some time, but there are still too many people being disconnected from games and desynced with the servers during matches.  Not as bad as it has been at times in the past, but still bad enough to be frustrating at times.
As new features have been added, there have been some annoying interface bugs introduced.  They don't really prevent enjoying the game, but they are a bit annoying.
Keep in mind that we are the Alpha Testers...so there are bound to be bugs.  They don't ruin the experience for me because I realize that players are the reason we lose...rarely is it because of the bugs.
If you like Lego blocks and you like to play multiplayer, there isn't anything much better than this.  I was a Minecraft junkie for quite a few years.  But I enjoy Robocraft so much that Minecraft only gets started up maybe once every 2 months.  I can honestly say that this is my favorite game of all time...and I've been playing video games for over 30 years.
To be completely transparent, I am a moderator for Robocraft.  However, moderators in RC receive no compensation: no perks, no pay, just tools to help manage game fairness and enjoyability.  If I ever stop enjoying Robocraft, you'll be one of the first to know as I'm not shy about my opinions once I have collected sufficient evidence to support them. This review has been updated several times already ;)

First off, let me say that i very much love what robocraft is TRYING to do.
As a young boy, i would often demolish my existing LEGO sets, and use the pieces to build giant killer robots (or at least so my imagination told me) and use them to spread glorious destruction and fireworks. It's gratifying to have a game that lets you relive those days, by building your own robot from scratch, and then using it to blow up other players.
Unfortunately, robocraft utterly fails on delivering on that fantasy. While the creative freedom in building your own robot is certainly there, that creative joy will soon get smashed to bits along with your carefully crafted creations, as you realize that creative robots, are often not very effective robots. Even those who try to design robots with a mixture of form and function, will find themselves frustrated, as the game's damage model means that special techniques are required to build efficient shells, and these shells will seriously undermine your aestethic sense.
On top of this, the weapon balance in the game is currently nonexistant. One type of weapons have all the advantage, and what little tradeoffs other types may have, don't even come close to compensating for the lack of firepower.
If you decide to play this game, you will find yourself up against opponents who half the time will be flying, and 80+% of the time will be using grenade launchers (plasma canons) as it is the only viable means of offence at the moment.
In short, while the game has the potential to deliver an experience of great creative and tactical freedom, it currently does not have that.
In short:
Pros
- Great fun to build robots
Cons
- Frustrating and unbalanced combat
-Instability issues with certain OS and hardware configurations
-Lack of tactical options in the game, both in terms of weapons and robot design
-weapon hit detection and game damage model is unwieldy and counter-intuitive to visual design and animations
The only reason to recommend this game at the moment, is to add your voice to the crowd of disgruntled players, or as a creativity tool.

Portal 2 is definitely a must buy. It is one of those games that hooks you in from the start until the very end and leaves that feeling of "i want some more" when you're done with it.
STORY
The story takes place after Portal 1 and is told pretty much alike: dubious, obscure, interpretative. You're constantly being manipulated by the characters in this game, and the few truths are to be found or concluded by yourself and/or outside of the test chambers, where you get to visit Aperture's offices and learn about it's creations and origins. Personally i love these kinds of storytelling because it opens so much space for discussion and secrets that it makes the game even more entertaining.
GAMEPLAY
It's basically a puzzle game that consists into figuring out the portals physics and how to interact with the enviroment around you and with other gizmos such as turrets, crates, the infamous Companion Cube, gels and so on.Some of them are quite hard and challenging. It's a better version of Portal on this aspect, and if you have played it and liked it, you're bound to enjoy Portal 2's gameplay as well.
CHARACTERS
I felt that creating this topic was important because the main antagonists in this game are AMAZING. Ellen McLain did and astonishing job on voicing GLaDOS. She annoys you, manipulates you, makes you angry, is ironic and has one of the smartest dialogue to be seen in videogame history. Definitely my personal favorite villain. And there's also Wheatley, a british-ish robot core that (SPOILER!) starts as a friendly guy but betrays you halfway through the game, so you end up seeing both of his personalities, even though he never ceases to be a moron and never ceases his stand-up-like jokes, which in my opinion makes him quite interesting, funny and enjoyable.
MULTIPLAYER
The multiplayer coop campaign is a great experience that adds to the replay value of this game. It's just as good as the main campaign, except that it requires two thinking brains and Portal guns. It even brighten up a little bit this game's story, so it's pretty interesting, and it's quite long too.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece. If you do not own it yet, i truly recommend it.
BTW: Someone please teach Mr. Gabe Newell and the Valve team how to count to 3. They might be lacking some basic math here and pretty much the entire community would like a third installment to most of their games, such as Portal, Half-life and Left4Dead. Let's make number 3 a reality.

Came for an amazing pancake recipe?
Than you came to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

I just finished the single-player campaign with only a few peeks at walkthroughs and it was the exact level of challenging + satisfying that I was hoping for. There is far more room for thoughtful, slow puzzle-solving (with bursts of exhilarating movement and aha! moments) than Portal 1 (which I revisited and, yeah, the earliest puzzles with shifting built-in portals and timed events are actually more difficult in a "man, this is annoying" kind of way).
Co-op is differently lovely and was incredibly fun, but having a more focused/experienced partner helped a lot. Sometimes my partner would figure out a path to the exit before I could figure out what was going on, so we'd leave and I'd be clueless. This lends a lot of replay value (the cutscenes are short and as usual, no respawn penalty, so restarting from level one doesn't seem daunting or exhausting), as with each different partner, you'll figure out different things in a different order with each partner having different or new strengths. Sometimes you use your partner pretty much as a moveable weighted cube, just standing on things or pushing buttons you're told to push while the other guy does all the thinking. Sometimes real collaboration and timing is a necessity. Balancing of each partner's strengths and weaknesses becomes a real aspect of the game and leads to actual, in-reality, relationship-building. Your frustration or reliance on (or competitive streak against) the other character carries over into how you cooperate in real life via voice comm to progress.
The access to Steam Workshop community maps makes this game endlessly playable, even if co-op may eventually wear thin after a few run-throughs with different people. There are some excellent maps out there, and ones which introduce different architecture than what you're used to--new approaches to vertical gameplay or problem-solving methods.

As the game has undergone extensive changes since I had reviewed the game last, I decided to go ahead and update my review, and attempt to play the game again, and leave a more informed, updated review.
Sadly, what I discovered was the game is still as broken as the day I left my review.
It gets points for originality, no question there, the concepts BEHIND it are fantastic.
The problem is....it doesn't really work. Not for such a "competative" enviroment like this. Some stuff works, some doesn't, weapons are HORRIBLY unbalanced. Good point for this was I was just running a particular Tier (T7) with T8 weaponry. I couldn't hurt enemy players, and then in a matter of seconds, not only were my weapons gone, but I was destroyed not much later. EVERY. TIME. Dying a few times, Ok, I get it, I'm playing poorly. Dying EVERY time I engage someone in combat? That's bull. Even worse, judging from their color, they were using the same armor blocks as me, so why exactly were my weapons doing so much Worse against their armor, while they were chewing mine to shreds?
Even worse, the ONLY WAY to get currency, is to either throw money at the game, or just get curb stomped by everyone and their mother until you can manage to save the credits (by loosing I'll add) that you can unload your own bot, and make currency that way.
Ultimately, I don't recommend this game. At all. Its got cool concepts, and its still fun to build random things, and see if they work. But the combat is broken. Heavily. And still is.

I just finished the single-player campaign with only a few peeks at walkthroughs and it was the exact level of challenging + satisfying that I was hoping for. There is far more room for thoughtful, slow puzzle-solving (with bursts of exhilarating movement and aha! moments) than Portal 1 (which I revisited and, yeah, the earliest puzzles with shifting built-in portals and timed events are actually more difficult in a "man, this is annoying" kind of way).
Co-op is differently lovely and was incredibly fun, but having a more focused/experienced partner helped a lot. Sometimes my partner would figure out a path to the exit before I could figure out what was going on, so we'd leave and I'd be clueless. This lends a lot of replay value (the cutscenes are short and as usual, no respawn penalty, so restarting from level one doesn't seem daunting or exhausting), as with each different partner, you'll figure out different things in a different order with each partner having different or new strengths. Sometimes you use your partner pretty much as a moveable weighted cube, just standing on things or pushing buttons you're told to push while the other guy does all the thinking. Sometimes real collaboration and timing is a necessity. Balancing of each partner's strengths and weaknesses becomes a real aspect of the game and leads to actual, in-reality, relationship-building. Your frustration or reliance on (or competitive streak against) the other character carries over into how you cooperate in real life via voice comm to progress.
The access to Steam Workshop community maps makes this game endlessly playable, even if co-op may eventually wear thin after a few run-throughs with different people. There are some excellent maps out there, and ones which introduce different architecture than what you're used to--new approaches to vertical gameplay or problem-solving methods.

Having around 30 hours of time put in to this game I finally feel confident in putting in a review. Robocraft is fun for many reasons, the building, the testing, the driving/piloting, and of course, the shooting. This game almost has something for every one. The building system is simple to pick up and make cool things with, you get rewarded for testing your skills and your machine in single player mode, the piloting is easy to learn but hard to master (depending on your type of vehicle), and the combat is unique. The game does a good job with keeping vehicles very unique, the flying and hover vehicles are hard to handle at times and even harder to build and the ground vehicles seem easier to pilot but tend to be a lot more tanky and easier to build. Different weapon systems are also a key part to the game, I personally strapped plasma cannons to the underneath of a plane to make a bomber-like vehicle that's loads of fun to use on ground vehicles but usually loses in a dog fight if the opponent has SMG's or any thing fast firing or shoots straight.
Now for the few bad parts. I've noticed that with the new update premium is now really emphasized. Now that the different armor types and colors are gone, you are given a new paint tool. It's a cool feature until you realize only 4 colors (I believe) are available to standard members. The new update also seemed to really emphasize mech vehicles making them much more affordable then other machines, and now not giving you a choice on what movement type you start off with. For new players the recent update just does not do the game justice in all honesty. Some thing I forgot to mention in the good parts about the game, friends are easy to find and play with. The only bad thing about the Platoon system is for some reason when in a Platoon (basically just a party) it seems to take A LOT longer to find games which is very frustrating.
With all that said, I believe the game shows a lot of potential (it is still early access) and I can only think that it will improve. I rate it a good 7/10.

This game has several problems with it that are currently not fixed. There are several bugs that can break the game that I've experienced, as well as problems with game design that promote cheese strategies. On top of that the game's ranking system is a bit broken.
The short version is: you will run into players more powerful than you because of bad match making (statistically better I might add), there is no tutorial and you will need to do research before really going into this game, and some multiplayer modes are broken (in the sense that they offer a less than fun experience because of poor design decisions, such as the optimal strategy is to rush the opponent’s base, and the only reason why you wouldn't is because it would be poor sportsmanship. Guess how many players that actually affects)
On top of all that, you will be hard pressed to get a premium account (Which is expensive) to get anywhere quickly (About $17.80 a month at its cheapest rate, which will demand that you put down 200$ to get. That's more than a sub to WOW which is $12.99 a month).
Not to mention the problems with getting upgrades and the progression system that further ♥♥♥♥s with multiplayer.
And the big cherry on top is that if no one buys a premium account, you cannot progress. That's right, if no one else in the matches that you player buys a premium account, you will not gain EXP to get more gear. (This is compounded that there are only 5 guns in the game, 2 of which you will be stuck with until level 15+)
I still play the game, I was surprised to find that because of the building aspect, I was able to look past all of these (Aside from the multiplayer problems) because it doesn't affect me as much. Although I will say that I'm more engaged with Minecraft (Which is cheaper, has more content, and doesn't actively ♥♥♥♥ over newer players.) Honestly I would say that you would be better off playing TF2. I've played so much of TF2 that I've kinda gotten sick of it (Around 1,500 hours or so.) and this game is a fresh change of pace, but TF2 kept me going for 1,500 hours, this game might keep my attention for maybe 60-70 hours.
Don't waste your time here, it has too many problems and I don't see it being fixed unless the players literally start leaving on mass, which at that point the game will be beyond dead because once your player base starts leaving, people aren’t going to come back. I could see that happening fairly soon with how expensive the game is.

As someone who's least two favorite genre's in videogames are Matchmaking combat games, and MOBA's, the combination of both in this game has been fantastic.  I think it's the oldschool MechWarrior fan inside of me that really draws me to this game.
Keep in mind that I am playing this game for the first time, AFTER this huge update they just had.  Evidently this changes the game quite a bit, some some oldschool fans hate it.  So I am specifically reviewing the "new" game.
This game is fantastic, it really is.  It's fun, casual, light, but with a component that allows you to be hardcore.  It had a lot of room for improvement, but I am really enjoying it.
Pros:
Diverse weapon / bot types, everything feels so different.
There's a definite learning curve.  Skill > Luck most of the time
Matchmaking is pretty balanced
CFR is an awesome idea (robot factory for buying/selling designs)
I mean... it's free.
It's just a fun game, I'll stop here because I could go on and on.
Cons:
I do not support microtransaction systems in games that have such appeal to children.  It's baiting at it's finest.
No clan system, this game would benefit immensely from expanding on the social aspect of gaming.
Maps are pretty limited considering how long the game has existed.
My only main gripe/con to the game is that it has been around for so long, and has such potential that I'm surprised there isn't more to it.  Like I said though, it's a great game, and it's free to try... so why not?

Very fun game if you enjoy building and still want an explosion or ten in the mix.  Was slightly irritated with the new update, as the game used to follow a tiering system.  Tiers 1 through 10, with each block being doubly as expensive as the last.  At Tier 10, the blocks cost 12k in game currency apiece.  The amount of time I spent to build a single 1100-1200 cube robot was immense; given that each match lasted close to 15 minutes, and each one averaged 60-80k.  With the most recent update, tiers do not exist.  You only get a single type of block that you can buy for 10 points.
Despite that, the game is still extremely enjoyable.  Experimenting with new builds, making something that no-one else can have except you, then showing it off by killing everyone who can't use it.  It's very fun and very worth the download.
Some other reviews I have seen call it a P2W game.  The only things you use GC (Paid Currency) for is not having to use RP (In Game Currency), very quickly accelerating your builds and tech.  You can buy cosmetic items, and even cosmetic guns and thrusters (Which function exactly the same as normal RP ones do).  As with all other "Pay to move faster" games, Robocraft was branded as "Pay to Win" when it really isn't.
Now given the game is still being worked on, there are bugs here and there (most of them hilarious).  Any that are found are generally quickly fixed.  Once had a spider walker that just refused to use its right legs, plopped over, then began spinning its legs in circles.  Sure it broke for that match, but I never saw the issue again, and got quite a laugh from it too.
Give it a shot, or maybe some more shots, depends on how many guns you get really.

If you asked me ANY Time last year or even earlier this year i would've said this is by far my favorite game, they removed teirs, they removed the pilot seat, they screw up the tech web so you're stuck with a tech pole, not even a tree. You used to be able to pick what things you wanted more than others, if you didn't want helium, you didn't need helium, they could care less. Now you get helium regardless of what you want.
That was just a scratch of what this review is. Now i will explain why each of those things was important.
-The pilot seat-
This used to be what you had to protect, you had to deal with the weight of it, engineer creative ways you could protect it from being damaged, now thats removed, what is there to protect? Guns? Wheels? Blocks?
-Tiers-
This was the "Leveling up". It was implemented a way i loved, you upgrade your blocks and guns, so that would count towards your new teir, as soon as you had enough of htose blocks and guns your teir would go up, now it's a level thing, A little to confusing to under stand as well. I belive as you hit marks you get new items.
Along with the removal of teirs came the removal of teired items, now it is a weird one item thing, where some guns get better as the price goes up? And are stupidly expensive.
-"Tech tree"-
The tech web, yes at one point is was a tech web, now you get one item after the other, so you are forced on the items you get one after another. You used to be able to pick and choose what YOU wanted, they had tech points you earned and with those you evolved your tech web, and you would get to choose what item you wanted, although eventually you would need to get the rest but you could get the stuff you wanted way before them. Now you are stuck with the spiral tech pole.
If they revert this stuff it will become my favorite game, but now, it's just not even fun to play. It's pointless, and dumbed down. It used to take skill, now you can spam blocks and actually still do decent. Out of my 50 games at the momment this dropped down from #1 to bottom 3 favorite games.

It used to be that you would build a robot of a certain tier, and would be matched with similar robots. Hearing complaints about how you could exploit the ranking system, they attempted to balance it, but it was a crap method of doing so: by completely removing the system. At this point, I stopped playing for a while. I came back to this game, hearing of a new update, and they had in fact removed features. You didn't need a pilot's seat, armor had been completely..."reworked," and they had made glass, which was SUCH A COOL-LOOKING BLOCK, into a freakin' cosmetic item! And the only way to get cosmetic items is with real money. Oh, did I mention that MOST COLORS OF PAINT YOU NEED TO PAY FOR?!
*sigh*

Portal 2 takes place in the distant future, after the events of Portal, and was released in 2011. Like the original Portal, Portal 2 is a First Person Puzzle game created by Valve. Again  you play as Chell, the survivor of Portal, who must once again use Aperture technology to escape. With the help of Wheatley, a personality bot, you have to overcome various obstacles in an attempt to escape through the delapitated testing chambers.
Portal 2 has a more indepth storyline than the original, and gives a little back story into Aperture Science and it's founder; Additionally, aside from Single player mode, Portal 2 also has a cooperative campaign mode. Portal 2 is as much of a fun puzzle game as the original, so if you enjoyed Portal, you should buy Portal 2, because it has better challenges and more story.

Full spectrum of autism, maybe. This game is a really good idea. In fact, it was a perfectly sound game at one point. It worked. People tried to make bots that did what they wanted, and the designs were original and actually quite ingenious. Over time, the common practice of creating builds that were cheesy and powerful came into existence, as it always does.
People found ways to get high tier gear into low tier matches. The director's idea of combatting this? Removing the one aspect that made efficient design a challenge- the pilot seat. Add in new parts. Change the mechanics. Now? Everyone rolls the same♥♥♥♥♥♥and charges into a 45-second match. Nothing original. No ingenuity, no self-respect. Just people playing to win. Simplifying and oversimplifying. Working toward gratification in victory rather than in development. In enjoyment.
Save yourself some time.

Together with its predecessor, "Portal 2" provides a very unique gaming experience, in which every single piece of the puzzling adventure is thought of, adding up to a game which achieves to constantly surprise the player by always finding a different way of approach.
Unlike many other modern games, "Portal 2" vehemently sticks to his roots and tries to preserve the purity of its self-consciousness, meaning that it acknowledges the possibilities but also the boundaries of its medium, while not trying to be the next "interactive movie experience" or some other hybridform of gaming. "Portal 2" mostly achieves this by creating characters, which don't strive to be perfect or overcomplicated. Instead their characterizations focus on basic attributes, resulting into giving tiny turrets, a ruthless A.I. or even an ordinary cube more personality than most of the other characters in recent video game history.
Besides its abilities to tell a sweeping story, "Portal 2" also doesn't fail to provide an exceptional gameplay experience, just by equipping the player with maybe the best designed device in video game history. To round up the package even more, the game inherents an excellent soundtrack, which seems to stay still alive in the players head, even after the credits have rolled.

At some point along the way this game transformed from a engineering survival game where you design a bot to protect a very vulnerable core to an FPS MOBA where construction of your bot is more of a cosmetic choice than an engineering challenge.
From there the game geared away from its roots, depreciating the value of your armor and choice of placement by removing the core you had to protect and adding in an autoheal mechanic. The gameplay turned from the slow tank-like bots carefully targeting key parts on the enemy to very quick and twitchy combat akin to TF2 and Overwatch.
Unlike TF2 and Overwatch however there are no classes to balance here, which has constantly been an issue where people engineer the best possible combination and you either conform to these optimized builds or be defeated by these builds in a manner that feels unfun and unfair. Effectively this means there actually are classes in this game which depreciates any engineering challenge in building a bot as the optimal solutions have already been discovered and their range is quite narrow.
All in all, this game actually isn't bad, but the developers have moved away from the engineering survival genre in favor for the twitch shooter genre and that simply doesn't appeal to me.
The grind is REAL. That, and with the removal of the pilot seat, the game's constructive and creativity is really distilled and dumbed down.

2014-present: Ever-expanding Team Fortress 2, and some cool added Steam features (like broadcasting). I see. Nevermind then!

When I had a chance to play Portal 2 at my friend's house one day, I knew this would have to be one of the first games I buy on Steam. Many puzzle games have the fault of being too difficult, unoriginal, and ultimately having low replayablility because puzzles you've already figured out once are no fun. This game throws all those faults in the garbage. While the game was very difficult, and I have been stuck on the same level for an hour once or twice, I never felt like the game was unbeatable, and I enjoyed it very much. The portal gun is also one of the most original game items I have ever encountered, and I never get tired of using it. Lastly, it is one of the most replayable puzzle games yet. For one, the co-op mode is very fun, and while even if you already beat it once, the experience can be completely different depending on who you play with, so it's always fun to play it with someone new. There's also the feature of community test chambers made by you, the players. Now you have to download the chambers, so depending on what computer you're playing it on, you can't just play community test chambers until you die, but it's always fun to see what other people come up with.

I've given this game a fair chance spanning almost 100 hours across endless patches and many months, and having spent way too many dollars on "premium" at times. In the end, anybody thinking to buy this game should carefully review the forums, which are mostly a mass of complaints about bugs, failures to connect, crashing, getting crashed out of matches, OP bot types that could be easily fixed by simple tweaks to the game physics that the devs just can't be bothered to do, and on and on.
In short, this game had tremendous promise, which is why I spent the hours and money on it. But, to do over again, I would not have invested either. And I'll say that the forums don't even provide a full picture of the frustrations you are going to encounter in your search for the realization of the promise of this game. You'll get sucked in by some initial fun and intrigue, and thus the promise hooks you. But before long you realize that the promise is a chimera and not to be actually realized. Then, like me, you'll look back at a lot of time in which only about 1/4 was having fun.
If you want to grind, it's "free to play," but your time isn't free, and you're investing it to have fun. Good luck with that. And DO NOT get on the money-treadmill. I know. It's tempting. But resist! If you're not having fun with the free-grind, you will not have any more fun by spending money. That just puts you onto a different grind.
Remember these words: the promise of this game is a chimera; it's a fictional beast that you will not discover in reality.

This game is as it is decribed. Build a robot, and bring it into battle.
It's moreso a vehicle arena combat game. Wheels, treads, hovers, wings, legs, rotors, and any combination of any.
Each weapon style is essentially a class.
From then on, you can build anything. I've made an Orca Whale healing hover. I'm made spider walkers. I've made a hover kracken. I'm made giant dongs covered in machine guns. I've made a few giant cubes and spheres. I've made a giant .44 magnum revolver. I've made a Johnny Five (is alive!).
The community can be fun, you can see very creative robots. Or you'll run into uncreative ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who copied an effective design off youtube. But that's with every game. Some people who play it for fun, some people who play it to fill an empty void in their self-esteem.
My ONE complaint that effects how I actually play the game is the disconnects.
EVERY battle, without except, 1-6 players disconnect. There will always be at least one.
In high level battles, losing your healer is almost always a certain loss if you aren't lucky.
I rarely feel like the battle is decided by skills. If the teams are decently matched, the battle is decided by a roll of the dice as to who gets disconnected, and which team is short-handed.
I have a great internet connection. I have tried all the tips online. I still get disconnected from 1/4 of battles. If I use a healer, I get disconnected 9/10 times. Upon contacting Robocraft, I get told that the client simply does not work well with many internet connections. On various forums, people get the same response.
Then I sign back in to get a two minute penalty for "leaving" the last battle early.
This game was and could still be my favourite if I could simply actually play it.
I recommend it simply because it is so fun to progress in, so fun to experiment in. And hopefully, it will work better for you. And hey, it's free.

**UPDATE** 1/14/16
I admit that the game is way better now since they brought back the battle arena and pit, but the reason I'm so negative about this game is due to it's change over time.
If you're a new player, you'll (probably) think this game is amazing, it has infinite possibilities on what you can create; and a nice progression system to follow too.
HOWEVER, if you've played Robocraft for a long time you'll probably dislike/hate it now. The reason behind this is that older players remember how the game used to be (before all these major changes and updates (like the old review I had below)). Robocraft used to have a progression sytem that let users choose what they wanted to buy from the "store" (by unlocking it in the "tech tree"); using a currency of "star coins" they earned from battle. Compared to modern day robocraft, you simpily unlock stuff automatically when you level up; whether you want that part or not. In the old game you choose if you wanted to unlock helium or a reflector pannel, but now you get helium reguardless of what you want (you have no choice of what's unlocked). The cubes (that you build your robot out of) are different too. Back in the older days, there were different "levels" of cubes, where some were stronger than others. Now they're all the same thing except with paint on them.
I myself don't necessarily hate this game, it's still really fun; but I dislike it because (as an old player) it used to be a much much better game than it is now.
**END OF UPDATE** 1/14/16
This game was a load of fun and excitement when I first got it off steam (Key word *WAS*). Ever since the huge update that changed everything, the game became a lot less interesting. Before the update, one could create any sort of robot they wanted and fight in either "team death match" or "Battle Arena". The game mode "Battle Arena" was a huge load of fun, robots had to stratagize and destroy the other team's towers in order to take down the main crystal tower; which would then blow up with a huge explosion during victory.
That gamemode has since been removed from the "lower class" and can only be played after you rank up high enough (approx 100 hours of gameplay). The only thing we have left is "team death match" which is basically pvp to the death.
It's still a lot of fun, but it gets bland after a while. Before you would have an option to choose what kind of game you played but now it's just one. Now, unless you level up to near max you can't play the fun gamemode.
The update ruined the game for lower-mid level players.

Robocraft is one of those games that is simple to learn, and difficult to master. The moment you boot up the game, you'll log in and be brought to your garage. From here, you can pick from one of three "slots" where you can store one of your glorious creations. From a bomber plane to a walking mech suit you can create the thing you can only dream of. If you can imagine it, chances are you can build it.
WEAPONS
Robocraft's weapon systems are split into families. Plasma launchers (AoE Bombers), Rail Cannons (Snipers), SMGs, Tesla Blades (Melee) and Nano-tech Disruptors (Healing/damaging beams) Every weapon has been carefully balanced with the others. A plasma launcher, for instance, can take upwards of six to seven seconds between volleys, meaning if your first shot doesn't disable your target, chances are you'll be dead. Rail cannons fire a single, high-power and high-accuracy shot from a distance, but can take upwards of twenty seconds between shots, meaning if you get spotted, you'll be blown to bits.
MOVEMENT METHODS
In Robocraft, there are multiple ways to move based on how you want your bot to act. Walker arms have spikes that let them spear into terrain and cling to walls and ceilings like a spider, granting extreme tactical advantages in caves at the cost of limited mobility. Mech legs are balanced and wont easily lose their footing, but are slow and take time to move from place to place, making any robot equipped with these effectively a towering behemoth. Hover blades let your robot hover around, at the cost that if any get shot off, you'll dangle lopsidedly and have a hard time moving if you do survive. Thrusters and helicopter blades help bots to fly, but have the same problems as hover blades. Get any shot off, and prepare for a world of pain as you struggle to keep control of your bot. And finally wheels are for fast movement on the ground at the cost of being unable to do anything else. Walker arms and mech legs can jump, too, which is quite useful.
IS IT WORTH IT?
In my eyes, yes. Robocraft has so many ways you can create a new robot that it has near unlimited replayability. Likely, you'll build your magnum opus and re-outfit it based on what you want to do at that time, and Robocraft will not protest or struggle, instead giving you the freedom to build what you want (So long as it won't topple over the moment the match starts.)
FINAL SCORE

Note: I started playing this after the despised update that apparently ruined the game.
Note #2: this review was written between the "league of mechs" and the "full spectrum combat" updates.
Things I like:
This is as much about building as it is about fighting. You build your robot out of blocks and guns. Only one type of gun per robot, tho, which limits the amount of thing you can do, but not enough to make the building part seem dull.
The matches: I have now been playing for 10 hours and my robot ranks about 1/6 of the score you need to have a second multiplayer mode. For a long time, you're going to have to stick with a single game mode: kill everyone in the opposite team or capture their base before they capture yours or kill everyone in your team.
For the moment, matches are on the rather short side, with a typical one probably lasting about 10 minutes.
Matches are fun, and shooting a bomber out of the sky or ending the spree of that one guy that has decimated your team feels quite rewarding.
I don't find the reward system inadequate, as now that I found a robot design that I like and can use well, I have no urgent need to improve it, and therefore do not need loads of cash in order to last enough in a match to be able to enjoy it. Also, the "average loading time" you see when in a queue for a match is pretty much the time you will actually wait. Often the match will start even earlier.
The only real problems I have are these:
- The CPU limit (basically a limit on the amount of cool stuff you can put on your bot). It's so darn low. I would have enough cash to cover my robot in shielding, yet I'm stuck with an ordinary tank because the CPU limit increases by a stupid amount per each level.
- Matchmaking: a bit weird. I am level 14 and keep finding myself against level 20+ players who have access to all kinds of upper tech and more powerful weapons. Kind of frustrating, though not game-breaking.
In short: fun if you do not wish to get to the "top of  tha best lvl max ever", and are just looking for a fun way to spend a spare half an hour. Can become boring after the fourth-fifth match in a row, but no-one says you must play 8 hours a day.
EDIT: crashes. Haven't had a single crash yet; however, as I only have 10 hours on this they might be awaiting me out there. The only annoying thing I encounter is the occasional lag spike, that, although brief, can make a difference between winning and losing a game.

Let me rephrase that in a more civilised matter. Robocraft, in its previous forms, while less developed, was more enjoyable and an overal better game. By previous version, I am refering to a stage of the game's development before the removal of the Tiered blocks and Megabots. Before the introduction of "over-powered weapons" such the missile launcher and flak-cannon. Before the game started going downhill.
However, after not playing the game for several long periods of time, then playing for bursts every few months, I have forgotten how good the game was before, and without this contrast visible in my mind, I must say that this game
enjoyable. The issue with the game was that many veterans of the game, such as myself in knowledge of what the game had been before, were able to be greatly disapointed by what the game has become as many great features of the game have been removed in place of more anti-consumer practices. An example of this is the removal of Tiered blocks. Originaly, armoured blocks in the game were of differing levels of damage resistence allowing them to be used as actual armour. However, the game now has replaced them with purely cosmetic cubes with only a small amount of colours available to non-premium players.
Do not misunderstand what I am saying. While I may apear "salty" with the changes made to the game, the truth is that the game was greater before, however the game is still good now. Despite this many veteran players are upset with these changes and will refuse to continue playing the game (excluding YouTubers who were either sponsered / endorsed or just financialy benefited from playing the game and uploading footage).

The tale of Robocraft is a sad one. A once great building and battling game that fell victim to popularity and feature bloat from devs.
The core game consists of making vehicles (robots) in a Minecraft-like style complete with a plethora of weapons, propulsion methods and utility blocks, then entering arenas and battling it out against other players online. I started playing the game in its youth and experienced it grow as more and more people discovered its simple yet addictive charm.
Unfortuately, with an increase in the number of players the devs started adding a lot to the game, fleshing it out and improving it in some massive respects, but losing the core values that initially made it great. Today there are a number of game modes and many more components than before, as well as a much larger playerbase.
I would still recommend this game, as it's still a good game, but it's no longer a great one.

This amazing sequel beats the original game by improving everything and adding more to the experience.
The story is continued and developed, giving more away about the history of Aperture Science and the main antagonist's story. Nothing feels forced or unnecessary, resulting in a story that gives just enough away and leaves just enough as a mystery for a satisfying end to the franchise.
There is a lot of comedic dialogue as well as intense and emotional scenes, as well as the voice acting, graphics, and sound effects all being improved. I also love the soundtrack, as it perfectly suits the environment and atmosphere that the game is going for.
The puzzles develop from easy to very hard just slowly and gradually enough for you to master the logic behind solving each one, resulting in you being fully trained to take on any chamber by the end of the game.
There is always something to be doing in this game. While some games seem to be over as soon as you finish the playthrough, Portal 2 gives you Co-Op mode after you finish the singleplayer story (in which you play with a friend or a stranger.) After that is done, you can create your own test chambers (for co-op AND singleplayer) or you can play the ones made by your friends and the community.
Although Portal 2 isn't a game that I play all the time, it will always be a source of nostalgia for me (since it was the first decent game I played all the way through.) The game is perfect for what it's intended to be, and every few months I end up coming back to it.

One of the greatest games of all time on PC, and certainly my favourite. The puzzles are great, improving on the original game. The story also manages to be even better, with awesome dialogue and voice acting by every single party involved (some may surprise you!) and this makes one of the coolest video game experiences available on the platform.
The storyline that spans both games is cleverly written and (this is important) takes you on an adventure. You are always progressing. To say much more than that would be to spoil the experience, but you are absolutely involved in everything, and the game puts you in the position to experience it. The narrative is interesting, the visuals manage to strike out in such a way that the setpieces become timeless and memorable.
Some assert that Half Life 2 is the greatest PC game of all time, but I never got much out of it. Portal is the Valve franchise I came to love however, and it's the one that's aged much better, both in terms of gameplay and storytelling. It's more than a puzzle gimmick game that spawned a few legacy internet memes, it's the best FPS singleplayer experience involving robots and portals you'll ever run into and a shining star on the platform it graces.

Gameplay- It gives you very little to play with at the outset but as the game pushes forward it gets a lot harder and gives you more means to complete the chambers. Let me start off by saying that I am a huge Valve fan. I love everything Valve, and so my review might be a little biased. But I don't think that really matters when everyone thinks the same about this puzzle solving game.
First, let's talk graphics. I've tried out the original Portal demo before ever playing Portal 2, and when I saw the graphics in Portal 2 I was honestly stunned. It looked amazing for it's time and it still holds up pretty well today, considering the fact that it was made 4 years ago, in 2011. While it may not look as good as most titles from the years between the game's release and now, I believe that the graphics has done it's job perfectly. It creates an atmosphere that almost makes you feel like you're there, trapped within the Aperture Laboratories with the rogue A.I. GLaDOS as you solve puzzles to try and escape the facility.
Now we move on to gameplay. If you've played the original Portal, then this would feel similar, but different. Valve has made many tweaks to the movement and the portal mechanics. An example of this is the fact that portals no longer actually travel, they just appear when you shoot them instead of flying through the air like in the original. This prevents you from shooting a portal in a portal like the original. The gel mechanic added quite a bit to Portal 2. It gave the players a way to alter your usual movement in the form of 3 gels: Repulsion Gel, that is blue in color and allows you to bounce on it to reach higher elevations; Propulsion Gel, that is orange in color and speeds you up when running across the gel; and Conversion Gel, which is white in color and allows you to place a Portal on any surface that the gel covers. These 3 gels add variety to the game, without completely straying away from the fact that it's mainly about the portals.
The sound. The sound design in this game is superb. It adds to the atmosphere that the graphics visually create, without being too over the top. All the ambient noises you hear while walking through the ruined facility, the dripping water, falling rocks... it all feels like it's actually there. The music is amazing too. It perfectly fits the puzzles you are solving and are nice to listen to when thinking. It's so good that I listen to it in my spare time (or maybe I just love Soundtrack.)
Now to the final part, the story. The story, that was nearly non-existant in the first game, became a huge narrative with a ton of lore of its own; and as Valve has shown, time and time again, that they are excellent at crafting lore. Every character got a backstory, be it with the dialogue, the secrets in the game or even the comic that Valve released. It became a great story that matched the puzzle game mechanics of equal proportions. The characters that Valve had created were so rich in personality, I couldn't help but play the game again and again just to see those characters again.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys atmospheric environments, puzzle solving, and lore.
If I had to give a final verdict, it would be none other than a 10/10.

Here is a cake recipe:
1 1/2 cups (3 sticks) unsalted butter, plus more for pans
3/4 cup Dutch-process cocoa powder, plus more for pans
1/2 cup boiling water
2 1/4 cups sugar
1 tablespoon pure vanilla extract
4 large eggs, lightly beaten
3 cups sifted cake flour (not self-rising)
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup milk
Mrs. Milman's Chocolate Frosting
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Arrange two racks in center of oven. Butter three 8-by-2-inch round cake pans; line bottoms with parchment. Dust bottoms and sides of pans with cocoa powder; tap out any excess. Sift cocoa into a medium bowl, and whisk in boiling water. Set aside to cool.
In the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, cream butter on low speed until light and fluffy. Gradually beat in sugar until light and fluffy, 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down sides twice. Beat in vanilla. Drizzle in eggs, a little at a time, beating between each addition until the batter is no longer slick, scraping down the sides twice.
In a large bowl, sift together flour, baking soda, and salt. Whisk milk into reserved cocoa mixture. With mixer on low speed, alternately add flour and cocoa mixtures to the batter, a little of each at a time, starting and ending with flour mixture.
Divide batter evenly among the three prepared pans. Bake until a cake tester inserted into center of each layer comes out clean, 35 to 45 minutes, rotating the pans for even baking. Transfer layers to wire racks; let cool, 15 minutes. Turn out cakes, and return to racks, tops up, until completely cool.
Remove parchment from bottoms of cakes. Reserve the prettiest layer for the top. Place one cake layer on a serving platter; spread 1 1/2 cups chocolate frosting over the top. Add the second cake layer, and spread with another 1 1/2 cups frosting. Top with third cake layer. Cover outside of cake with the remaining 3 cups frosting. Serve.

This was my first Steam game that I purchased 2 years ago. This game is what started my PC gaming. It took me awhile to play the campaign all the way through though. I have not completed the original Portal, but if you know anything about it, you should know that it was an amazing game just like this one.
The single-player missions revolve around you (Chell) working through test chambers to escape the testing. The chambers you go through have specific white walls were you can shoot your blue and orange portals. Going through the blue makes you come out the orange and vice-versa, or as the game describes it, “Thingy goes in, thingy goes out.” With the addition of gels; speed gels, bouncy gels, and gels that make unportable(?) walls portable(?) the puzzles can be made more difficult. The difficulty starts pretty easy and gradually gets harder as you progress. I don’t want to give away what any of the story is, but it is pretty cool.
The multi-player missions are where two robots, Atlas and P-body, have all the same concepts except the puzzles require use of 4 portals and occasionally the gels. There are only 5 main chapters each with 8 or 9 chambers, but when you complete all of those, you unlock a special chapter with 9 difficult chambers. The difficulty is amped up extremely from chapter 5 to the extra chapter, but it is still fun to play with a friend. I actually beat the coop campaign twice with two of my brothers (ToxicIrishman and GamerOfAllTrades).
Overall this is one of my favorite, and most well designed games I have played on my computer. It has good puzzles, great/humorous story, and fun gameplay.

2 h 12 servings 465 cals CAKE: 1 (18.25 ounce) package moist white cake mix 1 teaspoon instant coffee powder 1/4 cup
coffee 1 tablespoon coffee flavored liqueur FILLING: 1 (8 ounce) container mascarpone cheese 1/2 cup confectioners'
sugar 2 tablespoons coffee flavored liqueur FROSTING: 2 cups heavy cream 1/4 cup confectioners' sugar 2 tablespoons
coffee flavored liqueur GARNISH: 2 tablespoons unsweetened cocoa powder 1 (1 ounce) square semisweet chocolate
Prep
5 m
Cook
20 m
Ready In
2 h
Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease and flour 3 (9 inch) pans.
Prepare the cake mix according to package directions. Divide two thirds of batter between 2 pans. Stir instant coffee into remaining batter; pour into remaining pan.
Bake in the preheated oven for 20 to 25 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean. Let cool in pan for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and cool completely. In a measuring cup, combine brewed coffee and 1 tablespoon coffee liqueur; set aside.
To make the filling: In a small bowl, using an electric mixer set on low speed, combine mascarpone, 1/2 cup confectioners' sugar and 2 tablespoons coffee liqueur; beat just until smooth. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate.
To make the frosting: In a medium bowl, using an electric mixer set on medium-high speed, beat the cream, 1/4 cup confectioners' sugar and 2 tablespoons coffee liqueur until stiff. Fold 1/2 cup of cream mixture into filling mixture.
To assemble the cake: Place one plain cake layer on a serving plate. Using a thin skewer, poke holes in cake, about 1 inch apart. Pour one third of reserved coffee mixture over cake, then spread with half of the filling mixture. Top with coffee-flavored cake layer; poke holes in cake. Pour another third of the coffee mixture over the second layer and spread with the remaining filling. Top with remaining cake layer; poke holes in cake. Pour remaining coffee mixture on top. Spread sides and top of cake with frosting. Place cocoa in a sieve and lightly dust top of cake. Garnish with chocolate curls. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes before serving.
To make the chocolate curls, use a vegetable peeler and run it down the edge of the chocolate bar.

Here is a cake recipe:
1 1/2 cups (3 sticks) unsalted butter, plus more for pans
3/4 cup Dutch-process cocoa powder, plus more for pans
1/2 cup boiling water
2 1/4 cups sugar
1 tablespoon pure vanilla extract
4 large eggs, lightly beaten
3 cups sifted cake flour (not self-rising)
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup milk
Mrs. Milman's Chocolate Frosting
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Arrange two racks in center of oven. Butter three 8-by-2-inch round cake pans; line bottoms with parchment. Dust bottoms and sides of pans with cocoa powder; tap out any excess. Sift cocoa into a medium bowl, and whisk in boiling water. Set aside to cool.
In the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, cream butter on low speed until light and fluffy. Gradually beat in sugar until light and fluffy, 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down sides twice. Beat in vanilla. Drizzle in eggs, a little at a time, beating between each addition until the batter is no longer slick, scraping down the sides twice.
In a large bowl, sift together flour, baking soda, and salt. Whisk milk into reserved cocoa mixture. With mixer on low speed, alternately add flour and cocoa mixtures to the batter, a little of each at a time, starting and ending with flour mixture.
Divide batter evenly among the three prepared pans. Bake until a cake tester inserted into center of each layer comes out clean, 35 to 45 minutes, rotating the pans for even baking. Transfer layers to wire racks; let cool, 15 minutes. Turn out cakes, and return to racks, tops up, until completely cool.
Remove parchment from bottoms of cakes. Reserve the prettiest layer for the top. Place one cake layer on a serving platter; spread 1 1/2 cups chocolate frosting over the top. Add the second cake layer, and spread with another 1 1/2 cups frosting. Top with third cake layer. Cover outside of cake with the remaining 3 cups frosting. Serve.

I recommend this game but im going to give both Good and Bad things about this game.
Good:
-If you have a good imagination and taste of war then you can pretty much make the ultimate killing machine.
-You have the ability to test your machine before going into a real match. The A.I. mostly run than fight so you can test out your weapons.
-Lots of powerful weapons and upgrades you can do to your machine.
-Kinda inbetween but you do have to work and level up and earn money to get your upgrades. But this is a good thing because if you could everything at the start you could be facing up with people with some OP stuff.
-When you get to a certain level you are put into an upgraded version of the gameone you were just in. This adds some towers that upgrade your core including a regeneration shield around the core to repair yourself. It also absorbs enemy attacks. But to get the shield you need to have all the towers captured for your team. Becareful though because enemies can take them away from you.
Bad:
-Ok kinda inbetween again but there is a limit to how much stuff you can put on your vehicle. Now this is good so you don't face against someone OP but this is mostly bad because you have to level up in order to add more stuff to your vehicle.
-A shot to your driver is almost an instant kill depending on how strong the weapon is.
-A bit of bugs but this game is an Early Access Game so it is still in development.
-You and your friend have to be the same rank/level as eachother in order to play a match together. You can get around this by making a 2nd robot.
-If you happen to lose connection for a second and reconnect again. It doesn't kick you out, instead it makes everyone around you freeze and you can go up to a random enemy and attack them even if they kill you in game. You stay alive on your screen and can attack and kill any living enemy while is this state. But when game ends you finally get kicked out.
-If you have a special weapon like the railgun or the grenade launcher, then thats is the only weapon you can carry. So you can have as many little guns as you want but you can only have 1 railgun or grenade launcher with no other weapon on your vehicle? What makes this worse is that the railgun and grenade launcher despite being strong weapons. It has to recharge in order to shoot again. So you can only have 1 railgun or grenade launcher on your vehicle with no other weapon with it and it has to recharge in order to shoot again.
-Your vehicles can get heavy or light. So the more blocks and weapons you put on there your gonna get heavier. So if your trying to make a flying vehicle then you have some deleting to do.
-Remeber the regeneration shield iI told you about? Well even though it blocks enemy attacks, it actually lets them go right through the shield and attack from inside. You can do this too but it is kinda stupid that it can block attacks from the outside, but be able to go through the shield and attack from inside. I don't know why it doesn't keeps enemies from going inside too.
Conclusion: I even though it has both good and bad things, I highly recommend this game. Its fun and imaginative. Plus its free to play which is even better. So what are you waiting for? Go play the game!

My PRO / CON review atm:
Start with the bad things - CONs
o Building: you can use every item/every cube only one time
- so if you use a cannon on robot x, it´s not available to use it on robot y
o Free2play: this game is not pay to win, but there is a huge difference in possible progress between f2p and p2p gamers
- you can buy loads of loot boxes and have always top gear available
- you can get double the loot if you are a p2p customer
-> so it´s not impossible to get the top stuff for f2p people, but it´s quiet time consuming (it´s nearly impossible for my friedns to start with robocraft and catch up with me in an acceptable time)
o Gameplay: there are still some anoying things & imbalances
- short sight; on small maps like in this game, you should be abel to see enemys through a clear line of sight at all times! - in this game, it´s currently only half the map
- flyers, flyers everywhere ... god I hate those flyers -> maximum 1 or 2 flyers per team would be a nice thing!
And here are the + PROs (and = NEUT)
o Building: the old lvl-system with all the restrictions in using bots and stuff has been removed
+ now the bots have restrictions in cpu usage (max. 2000 or it´s a mega bot)
= the more blocks you use, the less weapon energy u have (mini cars with big guns ahead)
+ less cube variety, still all forms, but not every colour has a cube; now you can paint them your way
+ much more items available (shield, cloak, emp, gatling gun ...)
o Gameplay: it´s quiet fun to play robocraft atm!
+ interesting maps with a sophisticated topography
+ 3 game modes
+ ranked games for people who want to fight competitive with people on the same mmr
-> it´s quiet addictive gameplay (even if you ask yourself sometimes, how the people in your team can have the same mmr as you have :D)

Portal 2 draws from the award-winning formula of innovative gameplay, story, and music that earned the original Portal over 70 industry accolades and created a cult following.

Players will explore never-before-seen areas of the Aperture Science Labs and be reunited with GLaDOS, the occasionally murderous computer companion who guided them through the original game.
The game’s two-player cooperative mode features its own entirely separate campaign with a unique story, test chambers, and two new player characters. I can no longer recommend this game. It used to require thought and skill to build a good bot, now just slap anything together and add a lot of different guns and you'll do fine. And by fine I mean that you'll grind forever.
Also they added the "factory" which lets you buy bots. It seemed like a good idea at first but people just bought drones made by popular YouTubers. Drones were always my favorite thing to build - they were very challenging to make especially when there wasn't auto-healing. They had to be balanced and took a lot of iterations to get right. However, they adjusted the balance to make them easier to fly, and auto-heal, and then since that made them too powerful instead of changing the game back they just made it so that drones are really really slow.
Not interested in drones? Great! Just make a cube of guns or better yet attach three hovers to any large gun and you have the ultimate bot. Also since there is auto-healing and teams are only 4v4 there is no longer any teamwork required. Finally they changed the capture system from an innovative destroy-the-reactor to a very standard "stand on capture point" system that's totally unoriginal and uninteresting.
All of the interesting gameplay decisions that made this game fun in the past are gone in favor of loot boxes. LOOT BOXES. So infuriating. I'm honestly sorry that I ever spent money on this game :(
Old review from 2015:
This was my "go-to" game since it came out. It's pretty great, you build robots any way you like, and fight other players, 2 teams, in multiple game modes.
Game is fast-paced, skill-dependent, and fun with a group of friends. But, the player base and community are not good. There are plenty of players, and wait times to get in a game are short (around 20 seconds) however some of the players are very vocal and rude, and there aren't many community features to keep things together.
But, you can disable chat. Recommended.
